documents.fullTitle: Safe System of Work – Forklift Loading and Unloading
documents.html:
Document details

This safe system of work sets out how Pickard Event Services loads and unloads curtain-side trucks, vans and trailers by forklift. Every operator, banksman and visiting driver follows it, at Unit 1, Brickyard Road and on event sites where our forklift is used.

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
Reference SSOW-01 – Forklift Loading and Unloading
Locations Unit 1, Brickyard Road (loading area, yard and warehouse) and client event sites where Pickard operates a forklift
Task Loading and unloading curtain-side trucks, box vans, flatbeds and trailers by counterbalance forklift: pallets, stillages, flight cases, staging, aluminium profile bundles and event equipment
Persons at risk Forklift operators, banksmen, warehouse staff, visiting lorry drivers, contractors, visitors and anyone near the loading area
Assessor James Pickard
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner after an accident or near miss, a new forklift or vehicle type, or a change to the loading area

Key legislation and guidance: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999; Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER); Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 (LOLER); Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992; HSE L117 (Rider-operated lift trucks – operator training and safe use); HSE HSG136 (A guide to workplace transport safety); HSE INDG199 (Workplace transport safety – an employer's guide); DVSA guide Securing loads on HGVs and goods vehicles.

Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SSOW; makes sure resources, training and equipment are in place
Warehouse Manager Puts this SSOW into practice; authorises operators; checks records; stops unsafe work
Forklift operator Holds a valid certificate and written authorisation; carries out pre-use checks; follows every step below; in charge of the loading operation
Banksman / marshal Controls the exclusion zone; guides the operator and reversing vehicles where vision is restricted; stops work if anyone enters the zone
Visiting driver Reports on arrival; hands over keys or isolates the vehicle; waits in the safe area; does not enter the exclusion zone
All staff Keep clear of the forklift working area; wear high-visibility clothing; report hazards and near misses

Hazards and risk ratings

Risk = Likelihood (L) × Severity (S), each scored 1–5, as in the H-series risk assessments. Ratings are residual risk, with this SSOW followed. Collision with a pedestrian and vehicle drive-away carry the highest residual risk (5, Medium) because the outcome could be fatal.

Score Likelihood Severity
1 Very unlikely Trivial – no treatment needed
2 Unlikely Minor – first aid only
3 Possible Moderate – medical treatment, up to 7 days off work
4 Likely Major – RIDDOR-reportable or over-7-day injury
5 Almost certain Fatal or permanent disability
Risk score Rating Action required
1–4 Low Maintain current controls; review annually
5–9 Medium Controls adequate but monitor; improve where reasonably practicable
10–16 High Further controls needed before or alongside work; management attention
20–25 Very high Stop work until risk is reduced
Ref Hazard Main controls (steps in this SSOW) Residual L × S Rating
F1 Forklift striking a pedestrian or driver Exclusion zone, driver safe area, banksman, horn and lights, hi-vis 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
F2 Vehicle moving or driving away during loading Keys removed or held, handbrake on, wheel chocks where needed 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
F3 Load falling from forks or trailer when curtains are opened Pre-opening load check, curtains opened from the side, loads secured 1 × 4 = 4 Low
F4 Forklift overturning Rated capacity respected, level firm ground, loads low and tilted back, seatbelt 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
F5 Collision with the vehicle, racking or structures Clear line of sight, banksman, slow speed, layout kept clear 1 × 3 = 3 Low
F6 Fall from the trailer bed Nobody on the trailer while the forklift works that side; steps used 1 × 4 = 4 Low
F7 Long loads (profile, staging) swinging or striking people Spreader or fork extensions, banksman, extra clearance when turning 1 × 4 = 4 Low
F8 Load shifting in transit after loading Loads restrained to DVSA guidance; strap check before departure 1 × 4 = 4 Low
F9 Poor visibility (dark, weather, high loads) Yard lighting, reversing with a banksman, work stopped in poor conditions 1 × 4 = 4 Low

Before work starts

Competence

  • Only operators holding a current certificate from an accredited body (RTITB, AITT, ITSSAR or NPORS) for counterbalance trucks, and written authorisation from the Warehouse Manager, may drive the forklift.

  • Refresher training every 3–5 years, or sooner after an accident, near miss or poor practice.

  • Banksmen are briefed on the hand signals in this SSOW and on their duty to stop work.

  • At event sites, the operator also holds any venue permit or induction the venue requires.

Equipment

  • Forklift with a current LOLER thorough examination (at least every 12 months) and service record.

  • Rated capacity plate legible; attachments (fork extensions, spreader bars) marked with their own capacity and listed on the truck's capacity plate where required.

  • Wheel chocks, cones or barriers to mark the exclusion zone, and suitable steps for any trailer access.

  • Ratchet straps, load bars and edge protectors in good condition.

Personal protective equipment

PPE Who
High-visibility vest or jacket Everyone in the yard and loading area, including visiting drivers
Safety footwear Operators, banksmen, warehouse staff
Gloves with good grip Anyone handling straps, curtains or loads
Seatbelt (fitted to the truck) Operator, worn at all times while driving

Pre-use check (operator, start of each shift)

Check and record on the daily check sheet: tyres and wheels; forks for cracks, bends or wear; mast, chains and carriage; hydraulic hoses and leaks; brakes and parking brake; steering; horn, lights and beacon; seatbelt; battery charge or LPG cylinder and connection; capacity plate. Any defect = truck tagged out of use and reported to the Warehouse Manager.

Site set-up

  • Loading area firm, level and clear of debris, packaging and spills.

  • Lighting adequate for dark-hour working.

  • Pedestrian route and driver safe waiting area marked and clear.

  • Weather checked: work stops in high wind (curtains and long loads), ice, or heavy rain that affects grip or vision.

Safe system of work – step by step

Stage 1 – Vehicle arrival

  1. The driver reports to a Pickard staff member before opening the vehicle or leaving the cab, and is given the site rules.

  2. A banksman guides the vehicle into the loading position if it has to reverse or vision is restricted. Nobody stands behind a reversing vehicle.

  3. The vehicle is parked on firm, level ground with enough room for the forklift to work along the side and turn safely.

  4. The driver applies the handbrake, switches off the engine and hands the keys to the forklift operator (or locks them in the cab, with the operator's agreement) until loading is finished. Wheel chocks are fitted on any slope or where the trailer is uncoupled.

  5. The driver puts on a high-visibility vest and goes to the marked driver safe area, clear of the exclusion zone. Where agreed, the driver may stay in the cab instead, but never stands beside the trailer during loading.

Stage 2 – Set up the exclusion zone

  1. The operator sets out cones or barriers to form an exclusion zone around the forklift working area, at least the length of the forklift plus its load on each side of the vehicle being worked.

  2. The banksman (where used) confirms the zone is clear and takes up a position visible to the operator, outside the forklift's path.

  3. Only the operator and banksman enter the zone. If anyone else enters, the operator stops, lowers the load and waits until they have left.

Stage 3 – Opening curtains and checking the load

  1. Before releasing any strap, look through gaps in the curtain or from the rear doors for loads that have shifted or are leaning against the curtain.

  2. If the load has shifted, do not open that section. Tell the Warehouse Manager and plan how to make it safe (for example, open a different section first and remove the leaning items by forklift).

  3. Release curtain straps one at a time, standing to the side, keeping hold of each buckle so it does not whip. Slide the curtain back slowly and secure it so it cannot swing back.

  4. Remove load restraint straps and load bars only for the section being worked, and from ground level wherever possible.

Stage 4 – Unloading

  1. Operator puts on the seatbelt, checks the area is clear, sounds the horn, and approaches the vehicle squarely, at walking pace, with forks low.

  2. Check the load weight and centre against the rated capacity plate. If the weight is unknown or close to the limit, stop and ask the Warehouse Manager.

  3. Set the forks to the width of the load, insert them fully and centrally, lift just clear of the bed, tilt the mast back, and reverse out slowly, looking in the direction of travel.

  4. Lower the load to about 150 mm from the ground before turning or travelling. Never travel or turn with the load raised.

  5. For long loads (profile bundles, staging, trusses): use fork extensions or a spreader rated for the load, travel slowly, use a banksman to watch the ends, and allow extra clearance when turning.

  6. Place the load in its marked storage location or staging area, lower it fully, tilt forks forward and withdraw.

  7. Repeat for each item, working from the outside of the load inwards so the remaining load is not left unsupported.

Stage 5 – Loading

  1. Plan the load before starting: heaviest items low and over the axles, the vehicle's gross and axle weights not exceeded, items in reverse order of unloading at the destination.

  2. Lift the load from its location with forks fully inserted, mast tilted back, and travel to the vehicle with the load about 150 mm from the ground.

  3. Stop square to the vehicle, then raise the load only when stationary and close to the bed. Move forward slowly, place the load gently and lower it onto the bed (or onto bearers, so forks can be withdrawn).

  4. Withdraw the forks straight back without dragging or pushing the load, lower the forks, then reverse away.

  5. Place items tight to each other and to the headboard, so loads cannot slide. Use load bars, chocks or dunnage to fill gaps.

  6. Nobody climbs onto the trailer bed while the forklift is working that side. Where someone must go on the bed to position small items or fit restraint, the forklift is parked away from that side, forks lowered and key removed, and they use steps (never jump down).

Stage 6 – Securing the load

  1. Restrain every item or block of items to the DVSA load-securing guidance, using ratchet straps, load bars and edge protectors as needed. Curtains are not load restraint.

  2. Tension straps from ground level wherever possible. Check every strap for cuts, fraying or damaged ratchets; discard damaged straps.

  3. Close the curtains, fasten every curtain strap and buckle, and close and lock the rear doors.

Stage 7 – Completion and departure

  1. Operator parks the forklift in its designated parking bay: forks fully lowered and tilted forward, handbrake on, engine off, key removed.

  2. Remove the cones or barriers and do a final walk-round of the vehicle: curtains, doors, straps, nothing on the roof or tail lift.

  3. Hand the keys back to the driver, confirm loading is complete, and sign the delivery or collection paperwork.

  4. A banksman guides the vehicle out if it has to reverse. The driver leaves only once all staff are clear.

Hand signals (banksman to operator or driver)

Signal Meaning
Both arms raised, palms forward Stop
Arms beckoning towards the body Come towards me
Arms pushing away from the body Move away from me
One arm pointing left or right, other beckoning Move in that direction
Hands held apart, closing together Distance closing – slow down
Arms crossed in front of the chest Emergency stop

If the operator or driver loses sight of the banksman, stop immediately.

Never

  • Never operate the forklift without a valid certificate and written authorisation.

  • Never carry passengers, or lift people on the forks or on a pallet.

  • Never travel with the load raised, or turn on a slope.

  • Never exceed the rated capacity, or lift a load you cannot see over without a banksman.

  • Never let anyone walk or stand under raised forks or a raised load.

  • Never load or unload while the vehicle engine is running or the driver is in the exclusion zone.

  • Never push or drag loads along the trailer bed with the forks.

  • Never open curtains on a load that has shifted.

  • Never leave the forklift with forks raised, engine running or key in.

  • Never use a mobile phone while operating the forklift.

Emergencies

Situation Action
Load falls or starts to fall Stay in the cab with the seatbelt on; do not try to catch it; warn others; stop work and report
Forklift starts to tip Stay in the seat, hold the steering wheel, brace feet and lean away from the direction of the fall. Never jump out
Person struck or injured Stop all work; call a first aider; call 999 for serious injuries; do not move the injured person unless in danger; preserve the scene
Vehicle moves during loading Shout a warning; stop the forklift and move clear; do not try to stop the vehicle
LPG leak or battery fire Shut off the engine and the cylinder valve if safe; evacuate; raise the fire alarm; follow H19
Fire alarm Lower forks, park clear of exits, switch off and evacuate to the assembly point

All accidents, near misses and damage are reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day and recorded; RIDDOR-reportable incidents are reported to HSE by the Managing Director.

Related documents

  • Premises Risk Assessment – Unit 1, Brickyard Road (W1 Forklift operation, W2 Loading curtain-side trucks)

  • H5 – Working at Height (H5.7 Curtain-side trailer beds)

  • H8 – Manual Handling (H8.1 Loading and unloading)

  • H19 – Fire (H19.2 Forklift battery charging or LPG)

  • H21 – COSHH (H21.7 Battery acid, H21.8 LPG)

  • Forklift daily pre-use check sheet; operator authorisation register; LOLER examination reports

Monitoring and review

  • The Warehouse Manager observes loading at least monthly and records any corrections.

  • Daily check sheets and LOLER reports are kept for at least 2 years.

  • This SSOW is reviewed annually, or sooner as stated in the document details.

Sign-off

Approved by (Director): Mathew Pickard Date: 06/01/2026

documents.html:
Document control

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
SOP reference SOP-01 – Forklift Loading and Unloading
Linked SSOW SSOW-01 – Forklift Loading and Unloading
Version 1.0
Prepared by James Pickard (Managing Director)
Approved by Mathew Pickard (Director)
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner if SSOW-01 changes, after an accident or near miss, or when the equipment or task changes

1. Purpose

This SOP sets out the standard method for loading and unloading vehicles by forklift at Pickard Event Services, so the task is done the same safe way every time. The hazards, risk ratings and controls are in SSOW-01 – Forklift Loading and Unloading, which must be read with this SOP.

2. Scope

This SOP covers loading and unloading by counterbalance forklift, from vehicle arrival to departure.

Applies to:

  • Forklift operators, banksmen, warehouse staff and visiting drivers.
  • Unit 1, Brickyard Road (loading area, yard and warehouse) and client event sites where Pickard operates a forklift.
  • Curtain-side trucks, box vans, flatbeds and trailers.
  • Pallets, stillages, flight cases, staging, aluminium profile bundles and other event equipment.

Does not cover:

  • Forklift battery charging and LPG cylinder handling (see H19 – Fire and H21 – COSHH).
  • General forklift work not connected with loading or unloading a vehicle (see SOP-05 Forklift Operation).

3. Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Makes sure resources, training and equipment are in place; reports RIDDOR-reportable incidents to HSE
Warehouse Manager Puts this SOP into practice; authorises operators; checks records; observes loading at least monthly; stops unsafe work
Forklift operator Holds a valid certificate and written authorisation; carries out the pre-use check; is in charge of the loading operation; follows every step in this SOP
Banksman / marshal Controls the exclusion zone; guides the operator and reversing vehicles where vision is restricted; stops work if anyone enters the zone
Visiting driver Reports on arrival; hands over keys or isolates the vehicle; waits in the driver safe area; stays out of the exclusion zone
All staff Keep clear of the forklift working area; wear high-visibility clothing; report hazards and near misses

4. Definitions

Term Meaning
Exclusion zone Area around the forklift working area, marked with cones or barriers, at least the length of the forklift plus its load on each side of the vehicle being worked
Driver safe area Marked waiting area for visiting drivers, clear of the exclusion zone
Banksman Trained person who guides the operator or a reversing vehicle using the SSOW-01 hand signals and stops work when needed
Rated capacity plate Plate on the forklift showing the maximum load and load centre, including any listed attachments
LOLER thorough examination Statutory examination of the forklift, at least every 12 months
Load restraint Ratchet straps, load bars, edge protectors, chocks or dunnage that hold the load in place; curtains are not load restraint

5. Competence and authorisation

  • Only operators holding a current certificate for counterbalance trucks from an accredited body (RTITB, AITT, ITSSAR or NPORS), and written authorisation from the Warehouse Manager, may drive the forklift.
  • Operators complete refresher training every 3–5 years, or sooner after an accident, near miss or poor practice.
  • Banksmen are briefed on the SSOW-01 hand signals and on their duty to stop work.
  • At event sites, the operator also holds any venue permit or induction the venue requires.

6. Equipment, PPE and materials

Item Requirement
Counterbalance forklift Current LOLER thorough examination (at least every 12 months) and service record; passed today’s pre-use check
Fork extensions and spreader bars Marked with their own capacity and rated for the load
Cones or barriers Enough to mark the full exclusion zone
Wheel chocks Available for slopes and uncoupled trailers
Steps Suitable steps for any trailer bed access
Ratchet straps, load bars, edge protectors Good condition; damaged straps discarded
High-visibility vest or jacket Everyone in the yard and loading area, including visiting drivers
Safety footwear Operators, banksmen and warehouse staff
Gloves with good grip Anyone handling straps, curtains or loads
Seatbelt Operator, worn at all times while driving

7. Procedure

Follow these steps in order for every loading or unloading operation.

7.1 Preparation and pre-use checks

  1. Carry out the pre-use check. At the start of each shift, check tyres and wheels, forks, mast, chains and carriage, hydraulic hoses and leaks, brakes and parking brake, steering, horn, lights and beacon, seatbelt, battery charge or LPG cylinder and connection, and the capacity plate. Record the result on the daily check sheet.
  2. Tag out any defect. If any defect is found, tag the forklift out of use and report it to the Warehouse Manager.
  3. Check the loading area. Make sure it is firm, level and clear of debris, packaging and spills, and that lighting is adequate for dark-hour working.
  4. Check the pedestrian route and driver safe area. Both must be marked and clear.
  5. Check the weather. Do not start, or stop work, in high wind (curtains and long loads), ice, or heavy rain that affects grip or vision.

Hold point: Do not use the forklift until the pre-use check is passed and recorded, and do not start if the area or weather is unsuitable.

7.2 Vehicle arrival

  1. Meet the driver. The driver reports to a Pickard staff member before opening the vehicle or leaving the cab. Give the driver the site rules.
  2. Guide the vehicle in. Use a banksman if the vehicle has to reverse or vision is restricted. Nobody stands behind a reversing vehicle.
  3. Position the vehicle. Park it on firm, level ground with enough room for the forklift to work along the side and turn safely.
  4. Isolate the vehicle. The driver applies the handbrake, switches off the engine and hands the keys to the forklift operator (or locks them in the cab, with the operator’s agreement) until loading is finished. Fit wheel chocks on any slope or where the trailer is uncoupled.
  5. Send the driver to the safe area. The driver puts on a high-visibility vest and goes to the marked driver safe area. Where agreed, the driver may stay in the cab instead, but never stands beside the trailer.

7.3 Set up the exclusion zone

  1. Mark the zone. Set out cones or barriers around the forklift working area, at least the length of the forklift plus its load on each side of the vehicle being worked.
  2. Position the banksman. Where a banksman is used, they confirm the zone is clear and stand where the operator can see them, outside the forklift’s path.
  3. Agree signals. Use only the SSOW-01 hand signals. If the operator loses sight of the banksman, stop immediately.
  4. Control entry. Only the operator and banksman enter the zone. If anyone else enters, stop, lower the load and wait until they have left.

Hold point: Do not start loading or unloading until the engine is off, the keys are held, the driver is out of the exclusion zone and the zone is clear.

7.4 Open curtains and check the load

  1. Look before you release. Before releasing any strap, look through gaps in the curtain or from the rear doors for loads that have shifted or are leaning against the curtain.
  2. Release curtain straps safely. Release them one at a time, standing to the side and keeping hold of each buckle so it does not whip. Slide the curtain back slowly and secure it so it cannot swing back.
  3. Remove restraint for the working section only. Remove load restraint straps and load bars only for the section being worked, from ground level wherever possible.

Hold point: If the load has shifted, do not open that section. Tell the Warehouse Manager and agree how to make it safe, for example by opening a different section first and removing the leaning items by forklift.

7.5 Unloading

  1. Prepare to approach. Put on the seatbelt, check the area is clear, sound the horn, and approach the vehicle squarely, at walking pace, with forks low.
  2. Check the weight. Check the load weight and centre against the rated capacity plate. If the weight is unknown or close to the limit, stop and ask the Warehouse Manager.
  3. Lift the load. Set the forks to the width of the load, insert them fully and centrally, lift just clear of the bed, tilt the mast back, and reverse out slowly, looking in the direction of travel.
  4. Lower before travelling. Lower the load to about 150 mm from the ground before turning or travelling. Never travel or turn with the load raised.
  5. Handle long loads with care. For profile bundles, staging and trusses, use fork extensions or a spreader rated for the load, travel slowly, use a banksman to watch the ends and allow extra clearance when turning.
  6. Set the load down. Place it in its marked storage location or staging area, lower it fully, tilt forks forward and withdraw.
  7. Work from the outside in. Repeat for each item, working from the outside of the load inwards so the remaining load is not left unsupported.

7.6 Loading

  1. Plan the load. Put heaviest items low and over the axles, do not exceed the vehicle’s gross and axle weights, and load items in reverse order of unloading at the destination.
  2. Lift and travel. Lift the load with forks fully inserted and mast tilted back, and travel to the vehicle with the load about 150 mm from the ground.
  3. Raise only when stationary. Stop square to the vehicle and raise the load only when stationary and close to the bed. Move forward slowly and lower the load gently onto the bed, or onto bearers so the forks can be withdrawn.
  4. Withdraw cleanly. Withdraw the forks straight back without dragging or pushing the load, lower the forks, then reverse away.
  5. Pack tight. Place items tight to each other and to the headboard so they cannot slide. Fill gaps with load bars, chocks or dunnage.
  6. Keep off the bed while the forklift works. Nobody climbs onto the trailer bed while the forklift is working that side. If someone must go on the bed, park the forklift away from that side, forks lowered and key removed, and use steps (never jump down).

7.7 Securing the load

  1. Restrain every item. Restrain every item or block of items to the DVSA load-securing guidance, using ratchet straps, load bars and edge protectors as needed. Curtains are not load restraint.
  2. Check and tension straps. Check every strap for cuts, fraying or damaged ratchets and discard damaged straps. Tension straps from ground level wherever possible.
  3. Close up the vehicle. Close the curtains, fasten every curtain strap and buckle, and close and lock the rear doors.

7.8 Completion and departure

  1. Park the forklift. Park in the designated parking bay with forks fully lowered and tilted forward, handbrake on, engine off and key removed.
  2. Clear the zone and walk round. Remove the cones or barriers and walk round the vehicle checking curtains, doors and straps, and that nothing is left on the roof or tail lift.
  3. Hand back the keys. Return the keys to the driver, confirm loading is complete and sign the delivery or collection paperwork.
  4. See the vehicle out. A banksman guides the vehicle out if it has to reverse. The driver leaves only once all staff are clear.

Hold point: Do not hand back the keys until the forklift is parked and the final walk-round confirms the load is secured and the vehicle is closed.

8. Completion checks

Check Standard
Load restraint Every item restrained to DVSA guidance; no damaged straps in use
Load position Items tight to each other and the headboard; gaps filled; heaviest items low and over the axles
Vehicle Curtains closed and every strap fastened; rear doors closed and locked; nothing on the roof or tail lift
Forklift In its parking bay; forks lowered and tilted forward; handbrake on; engine off; key removed
Loading area Cones and barriers removed; area clear of debris, packaging and spills
Paperwork Keys returned; delivery or collection paperwork signed; daily check sheet completed

9. If something goes wrong

Situation Action
Load falls or starts to fall Stay in the cab with the seatbelt on; do not try to catch it; warn others; stop work and report
Forklift starts to tip Stay in the seat, hold the steering wheel, brace feet and lean away from the fall; never jump out
Person struck or injured Stop all work; call a first aider; call 999 for serious injuries; do not move the person unless in danger; preserve the scene
Vehicle moves during loading Shout a warning; stop the forklift and move clear; do not try to stop the vehicle
LPG leak or battery fire Shut off the engine and cylinder valve if safe; evacuate; raise the fire alarm; follow H19
Fire alarm Lower forks, park clear of exits, switch off and evacuate to the assembly point
Forklift defect found Tag the forklift out of use and report to the Warehouse Manager

Report all accidents, near misses and damage to the Warehouse Manager the same day so they can be recorded; the Managing Director reports RIDDOR-reportable incidents to HSE. See SSOW-01 for the full emergency arrangements.

10. Records

Record Completed by Kept by
Forklift daily pre-use check sheet Forklift operator, each shift Warehouse Manager (at least 2 years)
Operator authorisation register Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
LOLER examination reports LOLER examiner, at least every 12 months Warehouse Manager (at least 2 years)
Monthly loading observations and corrections Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
Accident, near miss and damage reports Person involved, same day Warehouse Manager
Delivery or collection paperwork Forklift operator and driver Driver and Pickard

  • H5 – Working at Height (H5.7 Curtain-side trailer beds)
  • H8 – Manual Handling (H8.1 Loading and unloading)

documents.fullTitle: Safe System of Work – Lone Working
documents.html:
Document details

This safe system of work sets out how Pickard Event Services staff work alone safely. Every lone worker checks in with a named buddy before and after the task, and remote CCTV is confirmed working before lone work begins at Unit 1. High-risk tasks are never done alone.

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
Reference SSOW-02 – Lone Working
Locations Unit 1, Brickyard Road (warehouse, mezzanine, yard, office), event sites, and driving between them
Task Any work where a person cannot be seen or heard by a colleague: early, late, weekend and out-of-hours work; opening and locking up; warehouse preparation; office work; site visits; collections and deliveries
Persons at risk Employees and agency or casual staff working alone
Assessor James Pickard
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner after an incident, a missed check-in that was not resolved quickly, or a change to CCTV or alarm arrangements

Key legislation and guidance: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999; Health and Safety (First-Aid) Regulations 1981; HSE INDG73 (Protecting lone workers – how to manage the risks of working alone); UK GDPR and the ICO guidance on video surveillance (for CCTV use).

Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SSOW; makes sure CCTV, phones and alarms are provided and maintained; appoints buddies
Warehouse Manager Authorises lone working; agrees the task and timings; acts as escalation contact; keeps the lone working log
Lone worker Gets authorisation; checks CCTV is live; checks in and out with the buddy at the agreed times; does only permitted tasks; stops and leaves if unsafe
Buddy A named, competent person who is contactable throughout. Receives check-ins; can view the remote CCTV; follows the escalation steps without delay if a check-in is missed
CCTV viewer The buddy, or another nominated person, with login access to the remote CCTV app

Hazards and risk ratings

Risk = Likelihood (L) × Severity (S), each scored 1–5, as in the H-series risk assessments. Ratings are residual risk, with this SSOW followed. The main danger of lone working is delay: an injury or illness that would be minor with help nearby can become serious if nobody knows. The buddy check-ins and CCTV are there to cut that delay.

Score Likelihood Severity
1 Very unlikely Trivial – no treatment needed
2 Unlikely Minor – first aid only
3 Possible Moderate – medical treatment, up to 7 days off work
4 Likely Major – RIDDOR-reportable or over-7-day injury
5 Almost certain Fatal or permanent disability
Risk score Rating Action required
1–4 Low Maintain current controls; review annually
5–9 Medium Controls adequate but monitor; improve where reasonably practicable
10–16 High Further controls needed before or alongside work; management attention
20–25 Very high Stop work until risk is reduced
Ref Hazard Main controls Residual L × S Rating
L1 Injury with no one to help or raise the alarm Buddy check-ins, CCTV, charged phone, first aid kit, high-risk tasks banned alone 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
L2 Sudden illness (fainting, heart attack, diabetic episode) Medical conditions disclosed in confidence; CCTV checks; escalation if a check-in is missed 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
L3 Violence or aggression (intruders, members of the public) Doors locked, CCTV visible, no confrontation, leave and call 999 1 × 4 = 4 Low
L4 Slips, trips and falls Good housekeeping, lighting on, no work at height alone 2 × 2 = 4 Low
L5 Fire while working alone Alarm working, exits clear, fire procedure in H19 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
L6 Fatigue and driving alone, especially after long or late events Rest breaks, journey check-in with the buddy, no driving when tired 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
L7 Phone failure or no signal Phone charged, signal checked, landline or alternative agreed 1 × 3 = 3 Low

Tasks allowed and not allowed when working alone

Allowed alone (with check-ins) Never done alone
Office and administration work Forklift operation, loading or unloading vehicles (SSOW-01)
Opening up and locking up Any work at height, including ladders, towers, MEWPs and mezzanine loading (H5)
Stock checks and tidying at floor level Lifting or moving items over 20 kg, long profile or staging decks (H8)
Light preparation of graphics and small items Using solvent-based cleaners in quantity, or battery topping up and LPG changes (H21)
Cleaning aluminium profile with detergent-based cleaners Hot work, power saws or other high-risk power tools
Driving to and from sites, collections of light items Electrical work, or work in confined spaces
Site visits and venue meetings Any task the person has not been trained for, or feels unsafe doing

If in doubt, the task waits until a second person is available.

Before work starts

Authorisation and fitness

  • Lone working is agreed in advance with the Warehouse Manager (or Managing Director), who confirms the task is on the allowed list and sets the expected start and finish times.

  • New starters, under-18s and anyone not yet trained in this SSOW do not work alone.

  • Anyone with a medical condition that could make lone working unsafe is encouraged to tell the Managing Director in confidence, so arrangements can be adjusted. Expectant mothers have an individual assessment before working alone.

  • Nobody works alone if they feel unwell, overtired or under the influence of alcohol, drugs or medication that affects alertness.

Buddy arrangements

  • A named buddy is agreed before every lone working period and recorded in the lone working log. The default buddy is the Warehouse Manager, with the Managing Director as backup.

  • The buddy must be contactable by phone throughout, able to view the remote CCTV, and able to reach Unit 1 or call for help if needed.

  • The buddy confirms they are available for the whole period. If the buddy becomes unavailable, they arrange a replacement and tell the lone worker before they leave.

  • The buddy holds the lone worker's planned task, location, start and finish time, vehicle details (if driving), and next of kin details from the staff file.

Remote CCTV

  • Lone work at Unit 1 only goes ahead when the remote CCTV system is confirmed live and recording, covering the warehouse, mezzanine stairs, office, entrances and yard.

  • The buddy (or another nominated viewer) has login access to the remote CCTV app on their phone or computer, and checks they can see live images at the first check-in.

  • If the CCTV is down or a camera covering the work area is not working, the lone worker does not start the task (or limits it to areas that are covered) until it is fixed or a second person is present.

  • CCTV is used for safety and security only, in line with UK GDPR. Staff are told where cameras are, CCTV signs are displayed, and footage is kept for no more than 30 days unless needed for an incident.

Equipment

  • Mobile phone, fully charged, with the buddy's and Warehouse Manager's numbers saved. Signal checked in the work area. Where signal is poor, the office landline or Wi-Fi calling is used.

  • First aid kit accessible; the lone worker knows where it is.

  • Lights on in all areas being used; external doors locked, with the alarm set to part-set mode where it has one.

  • Vehicle fuelled and checked before lone journeys.

  • A lone worker alarm or app with a man-down or panic function may be used in addition to buddy check-ins (see action in the monitoring section).

Safe system of work – step by step

Stage 1 – Check in before starting

  1. On arrival, before starting any work, the lone worker phones the buddy (a call, not just a text, so the buddy knows they are fine). They confirm:

    • where they are and which areas they will be working in

    • the task they are doing (from the allowed list)

    • the expected finish time

    • the time of the next check-in

  2. The buddy opens the remote CCTV app, confirms they can see the lone worker on live images, and tells them so. If the buddy cannot see live CCTV, the task does not start until the problem is fixed or a second person attends.

  3. The buddy records the check-in time on the lone working log.

  4. The lone worker locks external doors behind them, keeps lights on in the areas used, and keeps their phone on them (not left in a bag or vehicle).

Stage 2 – While working

  1. The lone worker checks in with the buddy at least every 2 hours, or more often if agreed, by phone call or by a text that the buddy acknowledges.

  2. The buddy may also check the live CCTV between check-ins, especially if the task is in a part of the building away from the office.

  3. The lone worker tells the buddy at once if the plan changes: a different task, a different area, leaving the site, or a later finish.

  4. If anything feels unsafe (an intruder, a fault, feeling unwell), the lone worker stops work, moves to a safe place, and calls the buddy or 999.

Stage 3 – Check out after finishing

  1. When the task is finished, the lone worker secures the building: equipment switched off, doors locked, alarm set.

  2. Before leaving the site, the lone worker phones the buddy to confirm the task is finished and they are safe, and gives an estimated arrival time if driving home or to another site.

  3. For long or late drives (over 1 hour, or after 10 pm), the lone worker sends a short "arrived safely" message when they get there.

  4. The buddy records the check-out time on the log and confirms the building appears secure on CCTV.

Missed check-in: escalation

If a check-in or the check-out is not received at the agreed time, the buddy acts straight away and does not wait to see if it arrives later.

Time after missed check-in Buddy action
At once Phone the lone worker. If no answer, text and phone again
Within 10 minutes View the remote CCTV and look for the lone worker in all areas. If they are seen injured, collapsed or in danger: call 999 immediately, give the address and what is seen, then follow the steps below
Within 15 minutes Still no contact and the lone worker cannot be seen safe on CCTV: phone the Warehouse Manager or Managing Director (escalation contact)
Within 30 minutes The escalation contact (or the buddy) goes to the site, ideally with another person, or arranges for someone nearby to attend. If attending is not possible quickly, or there is any sign of danger, call 999 and ask for a welfare check
On arrival Do not put yourself at risk. If there are signs of intruders or fire, stay outside and call 999
After the event Contact next of kin if needed (Managing Director only). Record what happened, and review this SSOW

For journeys, if the "arrived safely" message is missed: phone the lone worker; if there is no reply within 30 minutes of the expected arrival, phone the escalation contact, who decides whether to call the police with the vehicle details and route.

False alarms are fine. A buddy who escalates and finds the lone worker safe has done the right thing. A lone worker who forgets to check in is reminded, and repeated misses are taken up by the Warehouse Manager.

Emergencies

Situation Lone worker action
Injury Stop work; give yourself first aid if able; call 999 for anything serious, then the buddy. Stay in view of a CCTV camera if you can
Feeling unwell Stop work, sit down in a safe place, call the buddy. Call 999 for chest pain, breathing difficulty, or signs of stroke
Intruder or aggressive person Do not confront. Move to a safe, lockable place or leave the building; call 999, then the buddy
Fire Raise the alarm, leave by the nearest exit, call 999 from a safe place, then the buddy. Do not fight the fire alone unless it is very small and you have a clear exit (H19)
Vehicle breakdown or accident Move to a safe place away from traffic; call 999 if anyone is hurt; then call the buddy and the breakdown service

All incidents and near misses are reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day and recorded; RIDDOR-reportable incidents are reported to HSE by the Managing Director.

Lone working log

The buddy completes one line for each lone working period. The log is kept in the office (or a shared digital form) and checked monthly by the Warehouse Manager.

Related documents

  • Premises Risk Assessment – Unit 1, Brickyard Road (W14 Lone and out-of-hours working; O11 Lone working)

  • SSOW-01 – Forklift Loading and Unloading (never done alone)

  • H5 – Working at Height (never done alone)

  • H8 – Manual Handling (heavy and long loads never handled alone)

  • H19 – Fire (evacuation procedure)

  • H21 – COSHH (solvents, battery acid and LPG)

  • CCTV policy and privacy notice

Monitoring and review

Ref Action By whom Target date
CCTV Confirm remote CCTV covers the warehouse, mezzanine stairs, office, entrances and yard; give buddies app logins Managing Director Ongoing
CCTV Write a short CCTV policy and display CCTV signs (UK GDPR) Managing Director June 26
Buddy Set up the named buddy rota and the lone working log Warehouse Manager Ongoing
Alarm Consider a lone worker app or alarm with man-down function as an extra safeguard Managing Director June 26
Review Check the lone working log monthly for missed check-ins and follow up Warehouse Manager Ongoing
All Brief all staff and buddies on this SSOW and record signatures All Staff Ongoing

Sign-off

documents.html:
Document control

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
SOP reference SOP-02 – Lone Working
Linked SSOW SSOW-02 – Lone Working
Version 1.0
Prepared by James Pickard (Managing Director)
Approved by Mathew Pickard (Director)
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner if SSOW-02 changes, after an accident or near miss, or when the equipment or task changes

1. Purpose

This SOP sets out the standard method for working alone at Pickard Event Services, so that every lone working period is authorised, checked in, monitored and checked out the same way every time, with clear escalation if a check-in is missed. The hazards, risk ratings and controls for lone working are in SSOW-02 – Lone Working, which must be read with this SOP.

2. Scope

This SOP applies to any work where a person cannot be seen or heard by a colleague. The main danger is delay in getting help, which the check-ins and CCTV are there to cut.

Applies to:

  • Employees and agency or casual staff working alone, and the buddies and CCTV viewers who support them.
  • Unit 1, Brickyard Road (warehouse, mezzanine, yard, office), event sites, and driving between them.
  • Early, late, weekend and out-of-hours work; opening and locking up; warehouse preparation; office work; site visits; collections and deliveries.
  • Only the tasks on the “allowed alone” list in SSOW-02.

Does not cover:

The following are never done alone and are outside this SOP:

  • Forklift operation, loading or unloading vehicles (SOP-01 / SSOW-01).
  • Any work at height, including ladders, towers, MEWPs and mezzanine loading (H5).
  • Lifting or moving items over 20 kg, long profile or staging decks (H8).
  • Solvent-based cleaners in quantity, battery topping up and LPG changes (H21).
  • Hot work, power saws or other high-risk power tools, electrical work, or confined spaces.

3. Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Provides and maintains CCTV, phones and alarms; appoints buddies; backup buddy and escalation contact; contacts next of kin if needed; reports RIDDOR incidents
Warehouse Manager Authorises lone working and agrees task and times; default buddy and escalation contact; keeps the log and checks it monthly; follows up repeated missed check-ins
Lone worker Gets authorisation; checks CCTV is live; checks in and out with the buddy at the agreed times; does only permitted tasks; stops and leaves if unsafe
Buddy Named, competent and contactable throughout; receives check-ins; views the remote CCTV; records times on the log; follows the escalation steps without delay if a check-in is missed
CCTV viewer The buddy, or another nominated person, with login access to the remote CCTV app

4. Definitions

Term Meaning
Lone worker A person working where they cannot be seen or heard by a colleague
Buddy The named, competent person agreed before each lone working period who receives check-ins and escalates if one is missed
Escalation contact The Warehouse Manager or Managing Director, called by the buddy if contact cannot be made
Check-in A phone call to the buddy (or a text the buddy acknowledges, for interim check-ins) confirming the lone worker is safe
Check-out The phone call to the buddy before leaving site confirming the task is finished and the lone worker is safe
Remote CCTV The Unit 1 CCTV system, viewed live through the app
Lone working log The buddy’s record of each lone working period and its check-in times
Hold point A point where work must stop until the stated condition is met

5. Competence and authorisation

  • Only staff trained in SSOW-02 and briefed on this SOP may work alone. Briefing is recorded on the staff and buddy briefing record.
  • New starters, under-18s and anyone not yet trained in SSOW-02 do not work alone.
  • Lone working must be authorised in advance by the Warehouse Manager (or Managing Director), and only for tasks the person is trained for and feels safe doing.
  • Anyone with a medical condition that could make lone working unsafe is encouraged to tell the Managing Director in confidence, so arrangements can be adjusted. Expectant mothers have an individual assessment before working alone.
  • Nobody works alone if they feel unwell, overtired or under the influence of alcohol, drugs or medication that affects alertness.
  • Buddies are appointed by the Managing Director, must be competent, and must have login access to the remote CCTV app.

6. Equipment, PPE and materials

Item Requirement
Mobile phone Fully charged, with the buddy’s and Warehouse Manager’s numbers saved; signal checked in the work area; kept on the person
Office landline or Wi-Fi calling Used where mobile signal is poor
Remote CCTV Live and recording over the warehouse, mezzanine stairs, office, entrances and yard; buddy logged in to the app
First aid kit Accessible; lone worker knows where it is
Lighting On in all areas being used
Doors and alarm External doors locked; alarm set to part-set mode where it has one
Vehicle Fuelled and checked before lone journeys
Lone worker alarm or app Optional; may be used in addition to buddy check-ins, never instead of them
PPE As required for the allowed task being done
Lone working log In the office or as a shared digital form

7. Procedure

Follow these steps in order for every lone working period.

7.1 Authorisation and planning

  1. Agree the lone work in advance. Ask the Warehouse Manager (or Managing Director) to authorise it. They confirm the task is on the SSOW-02 allowed list and set the expected start and finish times.
  2. Check the task is allowed alone. If it is on the “never done alone” list, you are not trained for it, or you are in doubt, it waits until a second person is available.
  3. Check your own fitness. Do not work alone if you feel unwell, overtired or under the influence of alcohol, drugs or medication that affects alertness.
  4. Agree a named buddy. The default buddy is the Warehouse Manager, with the Managing Director as backup. The buddy is recorded in the lone working log.
  5. Confirm the buddy is available. The buddy confirms they are contactable by phone for the whole period, can view the remote CCTV, and can reach Unit 1 or call for help. If the buddy becomes unavailable, they arrange a replacement and tell the lone worker before they leave.
  6. Give the buddy the details. The buddy holds the planned task, location, start and finish time, vehicle details (if driving), and next of kin details from the staff file.

Hold point: Do not start lone work until it is authorised, the task is on the allowed list and a named buddy has confirmed they are available for the whole period.

7.2 Equipment and premises checks

  1. Charge and check your phone. Make sure it is fully charged with the buddy’s and Warehouse Manager’s numbers saved. Check signal in the work area; where it is poor, use the office landline or Wi-Fi calling.
  2. Locate the first aid kit. Confirm it is accessible and you know where it is.
  3. Prepare the vehicle for lone journeys. Make sure it is fuelled and checked before setting off.
  4. Set up the work area. Switch lights on in all areas being used, keep housekeeping good, keep exits clear and check the alarm is working.

7.3 Check in before starting

  1. Phone the buddy on arrival. Make a call, not just a text, before starting any work. Confirm where you are, which areas you will work in, the task (from the allowed list), the expected finish time and the time of the next check-in.
  2. Buddy confirms live CCTV. The buddy opens the remote CCTV app, confirms they can see the lone worker on live images, and tells them so.
  3. Buddy records the check-in. The buddy completes the log line, including CCTV live (Y/N) and the check-in time.
  4. Secure yourself in. Lock external doors behind you, set the alarm to part-set mode where it has one, and keep your phone on you, not in a bag or vehicle.

Hold point: At Unit 1, do not start the task until the buddy has confirmed they can see you on live CCTV. If the CCTV is down or a camera covering the work area is not working, do not start (or limit the work to covered areas) until it is fixed or a second person is present.

7.4 While working

  1. Check in at least every 2 hours. Use a phone call, or a text that the buddy acknowledges. Check in more often if agreed.
  2. Buddy monitors CCTV. The buddy may check the live CCTV between check-ins, especially if the task is in a part of the building away from the office.
  3. Report any change of plan at once. Tell the buddy straight away about a different task, a different area, leaving the site, or a later finish.
  4. Stay within the allowed tasks. Do not take on any task from the “never done alone” list.
  5. Stop if anything feels unsafe. If there is an intruder, a fault, or you feel unwell, stop work, move to a safe place, and call the buddy or 999.
  6. Manage fatigue before driving. Take rest breaks and do not drive when tired.

7.5 Check out and travel

  1. Secure the building. Switch equipment off, lock the doors and set the alarm.
  2. Phone the buddy before leaving. Confirm the task is finished and you are safe, and give an estimated arrival time if driving home or to another site.
  3. Buddy records the check-out. The buddy enters the check-out time on the log and confirms the building appears secure on CCTV.
  4. Send “arrived safely” for long or late drives. For drives over 1 hour, or after 10 pm, send a short “arrived safely” message to the buddy when you get there.

Hold point: Do not leave site until the check-out call has been made and acknowledged by the buddy.

7.6 Missed check-in escalation (buddy)

  1. Act straight away. If a check-in or the check-out is not received at the agreed time, do not wait to see if it arrives later. Phone the lone worker; if no answer, text and phone again.
  2. View the CCTV within 10 minutes. Look for the lone worker in all areas. If they are seen injured, collapsed or in danger, call 999 immediately, give the address and what is seen, then continue these steps.
  3. Escalate within 15 minutes. If there is still no contact and the lone worker cannot be seen safe on CCTV, phone the Warehouse Manager or Managing Director.
  4. Attend within 30 minutes. The escalation contact (or the buddy) goes to the site, ideally with another person, or arranges for someone nearby to attend. If attending is not possible quickly, or there is any sign of danger, call 999 and ask for a welfare check.
  5. Stay safe on arrival. Do not put yourself at risk. If there are signs of intruders or fire, stay outside and call 999.
  6. Escalate missed journey messages. If an “arrived safely” message is missed, phone the lone worker. If there is no reply within 30 minutes of the expected arrival, phone the escalation contact, who decides whether to call the police with the vehicle details and route.
  7. Close out. The Managing Director contacts next of kin if needed. Record what happened and review SSOW-02.

Hold point: Never ignore a missed check-in; continue escalating until the lone worker is confirmed safe. False alarms are fine.

8. Completion checks

Check Standard
Authorisation Lone work agreed in advance; task on the allowed list
Buddy Named buddy recorded on the log and available throughout
CCTV Confirmed live at the first check-in and recorded Y on the log
Check-ins Made at least every 2 hours and acknowledged
Building Equipment off, doors locked, alarm set; secure on CCTV
Check-out Phone call made before leaving; time recorded on the log
Journey “Arrived safely” sent for drives over 1 hour or after 10 pm

9. If something goes wrong

Situation Action
Injury Stop work; give yourself first aid if able; call 999 for anything serious, then the buddy. Stay in view of a CCTV camera if you can
Feeling unwell Stop work, sit down in a safe place, call the buddy. Call 999 for chest pain, breathing difficulty or signs of stroke
Intruder or aggressive person Do not confront. Move to a safe, lockable place or leave the building; call 999, then the buddy
Fire Raise the alarm, leave by the nearest exit, call 999 from a safe place, then the buddy. Do not fight the fire alone unless it is very small and you have a clear exit (H19)
Vehicle breakdown or accident Move to a safe place away from traffic; call 999 if anyone is hurt; then call the buddy and the breakdown service
CCTV down or camera not working Do not start, or limit work to covered areas, until fixed or a second person is present
Phone failure or no signal Use the office landline or Wi-Fi calling to contact the buddy
Missed check-in Buddy follows the escalation steps in 7.6 without delay

All incidents and near misses are reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day and recorded; RIDDOR-reportable incidents are reported to HSE by the Managing Director. See SSOW-02 – Lone Working for the full emergency and escalation arrangements.

10. Records

Record Completed by Kept by
Lone working log (one line per lone working period) Buddy Warehouse Manager; kept in the office or a shared digital form and checked monthly for missed check-ins
Buddy rota Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
Incident and near miss reports Lone worker or buddy, same day Warehouse Manager; RIDDOR reports made to HSE by the Managing Director
CCTV footage Remote CCTV system Managing Director; kept no more than 30 days unless needed for an incident
Staff and buddy briefing record Staff and buddies With SSOW-02 sign-off

documents.html:
Document details

This safe system of work sets out which personal protective equipment (PPE) Pickard Event Services staff wear, when, and how it is issued, checked and replaced. Hi-vis and safety footwear are worn at all times in the warehouse, yard and on build and break; gloves and respirators are worn for the tasks listed; and hard hats are worn whenever overhead work is in progress.

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
Reference SSOW-03 – Personal Protective Equipment
Locations Unit 1, Brickyard Road (warehouse, mezzanine, loading area, yard, office) and client event sites (venues, exhibition halls, outdoor sites)
PPE covered High-visibility clothing; safety footwear with protective toe caps; gloves (general handling, cut-resistant, chemical-resistant); respiratory protective equipment (RPE); safety helmets (hard hats). Eye protection is included where a task needs it
Persons covered Employees, agency or casual crew, subcontractors and visitors entering work areas
Assessor James Pickard
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner after an incident, a new task or substance, a venue rule change, or a change in the PPE supplied

PPE is the last line of defence. It is used alongside, not instead of, the controls in the H-series risk assessments and other safe systems of work (exclusion zones, extraction, mechanical aids).

Key legislation and guidance: Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992 (as amended 2022, which extends PPE duties to limb (b) workers such as casual crew); Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999; COSHH Regulations 2002 (RPE); Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 as applied to event build and break; HSE INDG174 (PPE at work – a brief guide); HSE HSG53 (Respiratory protective equipment at work); HSE INDG479 (Guidance on respiratory protective equipment fit testing); The Purple Guide to health, safety and welfare at events.

Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SSOW; provides suitable PPE free of charge; makes sure enough stock is held
Warehouse Manager Issues PPE and keeps the issue record; arranges face-fit testing; checks PPE is worn; replaces damaged PPE; stops work where PPE is missing
Crew chief / supervisor on site Briefs PPE requirements at the start of each job; sets and signs overhead work zones; checks PPE before work starts
All staff and crew Wear the PPE required; check it before use; look after it; report loss, damage or a poor fit straight away; do not alter PPE
Visitors and contractors Wear the PPE given to them before entering work areas, and follow instructions

Hazards and risk ratings

Risk = Likelihood (L) × Severity (S), each scored 1–5, as in the H-series risk assessments. Ratings are residual risk, with the right PPE worn and this SSOW followed. Falling objects during overhead work and being struck by vehicles carry the highest residual risk (5, Medium), because the injuries could be fatal.

Score Likelihood Severity
1 Very unlikely Trivial – no treatment needed
2 Unlikely Minor – first aid only
3 Possible Moderate – medical treatment, up to 7 days off work
4 Likely Major – RIDDOR-reportable or over-7-day injury
5 Almost certain Fatal or permanent disability
Risk score Rating Action required
1–4 Low Maintain current controls; review annually
5–9 Medium Controls adequate but monitor; improve where reasonably practicable
10–16 High Further controls needed before or alongside work; management attention
20–25 Very high Stop work until risk is reduced
Ref Hazard PPE control Residual L × S Rating
P1 Struck by forklift or vehicle because not seen High-visibility clothing 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
P2 Crushed or injured feet from dropped loads, trolleys, forklift wheels; puncture from sharp objects Safety footwear with toe caps and midsole 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
P3 Cuts and abrasions from aluminium profile, panels, straps and packaging Cut-resistant or general handling gloves 2 × 2 = 4 Low
P4 Skin contact with cleaners, solvents, adhesives, oils, battery acid Chemical-resistant gloves (and eye protection) 1 × 3 = 3 Low
P5 Breathing wood or MDF dust, aluminium dust, solvent vapour or spray Respirator (FFP3 or as COSHH assessment), face-fit tested 1 × 4 = 4 Low
P6 Head injury from falling tools, fixings or materials during overhead work; striking head on low structures Hard hat in marked overhead work zones 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
P7 Eye injury from dust, swarf, splashes Safety glasses or goggles 1 × 3 = 3 Low

PPE requirements by area and task

M = mandatory at all times in that area or during that task. T = when the task row applies. – = not required unless another row applies.

Area or task Hi-vis Safety footwear Gloves Respirator Hard hat Eye protection
Warehouse floor and mezzanine (any work) M M T – – –
Loading area and yard (including visiting drivers) M M T – – –
Forklift operation and banksman (SSOW-01) M M T – – –
Office (no warehouse access) – – – – – –
Event site build and break M M T T T T
Handling profile, panels, staging, straps (H8) M M M – cut-resistant – – –
Cleaning profile with detergent or solvent (H21) – M M – chemical T – if COSHH sheet says – M
Cutting or sanding wood, MDF, profile M M M M – FFP3 – M
Spray mount, aerosols, solvent paints – M M – chemical T – if COSHH sheet says – M
Battery topping up, LPG changes (H21) M M M – acid / cold-resistant – – M – face shield
Overhead work in progress (towers, MEWPs, truss, rigging, mezzanine loading, high racking) M M T – M – everyone in the zone T
Venue or principal contractor rules Follow whichever is stricter: this SSOW or the venue's rules

PPE specification

PPE Standard Specification Replace when
High-visibility vest or jacket EN ISO 20471 Class 2 minimum (vest); Class 3 jacket for yards and outdoor sites in poor light. Yellow or orange, with reflective bands Faded, dirty so it no longer stands out, torn, or reflective tape damaged
Safety footwear EN ISO 20345 S3 (or S1P minimum indoors): 200 J toe protection, penetration-resistant midsole, slip-resistant sole (SRA/SRC). Steel or composite toe caps both acceptable Toe cap exposed or dented, sole worn smooth or split, upper damaged, or after a heavy impact
General handling gloves EN 388 Good grip, abrasion level 2 or above Holes, worn grip, or contaminated
Cut-resistant gloves EN 388 Cut level C or above (ISO 13997) for aluminium profile and sharp edges Cuts, holes or worn coating
Chemical-resistant gloves EN ISO 374-1 Nitrile, as stated on the product's SDS and COSHH sheet; disposable or reusable After each use (disposable); when damaged, swollen or contaminated (reusable)
Disposable respirator EN 149 FFP3 for wood, MDF and aluminium dust; valved for comfort. Face-fit tested to the specific make and model After each shift, or sooner if damaged, wet, or breathing gets harder
Reusable half-mask respirator EN 140 with EN 14387 / EN 143 filters A2P3 combined filters for solvent vapour plus dust, where the COSHH sheet says. Face-fit tested Filters at the interval on the COSHH sheet or when a smell or taste is noticed; mask when damaged
Safety helmet (hard hat) EN 397 Adjustable harness; chin strap fitted for work at height or in MEWPs. Not painted or stickered with solvent-based labels After any significant impact; shell cracked or brittle; past the manufacturer's expiry date (usually 3–5 years from manufacture)
Bump cap (low-headroom work only) EN 812 Protects against knocks on fixed objects only; not a substitute for a hard hat under overhead work As per manufacturer
Safety glasses / goggles / face shield EN 166 Glasses for dust and debris; goggles for chemical splash; face shield for battery work Scratched so vision is impaired, frame damaged, or strap perished

PPE is issued in the right size for each person. Anyone who finds their PPE uncomfortable or ill-fitting reports it, and an alternative is provided (for example, different glove sizes, wide-fit safety footwear, or female-fit hi-vis and hard hats).

Safe system of work – step by step

Stage 1 – Issue and training

  1. On their first day, every employee and casual crew member is issued, free of charge: a hi-vis vest, safety footwear, general handling gloves and cut-resistant gloves. Hard hats, chemical gloves, eye protection and respirators are issued to those whose tasks need them, or held as pool stock for event sites.

  2. Each issue is recorded on the PPE issue record and signed by the person receiving it.

  3. Everyone receives PPE training on induction: what to wear and when (the matrix above), how to check, fit, clean and store it, its limits, and how to report defects.

  4. Anyone who needs to wear a tight-fitting respirator (FFP3 or half-mask) has a face-fit test for that make and model by a competent fit tester before use, repeated when the model changes, their face shape changes (weight, dental work), or at least every 2 years. Wearers must be clean-shaven where the mask seals; anyone who cannot be is given a powered or loose-fitting hood respirator instead.

Stage 2 – Before starting work

  1. The crew chief or supervisor briefs the PPE needed for the job at the start of each shift or event, including any venue or principal contractor rules.

  2. Each person carries out a pre-use check of their own PPE:

    • Hi-vis: clean, bright, reflective tape intact, fastened.

    • Footwear: no exposed or dented toe caps, soles intact with grip, laces done up.

    • Gloves: right type for the task, no holes or tears.

    • Respirator: correct type and filter, straps and valve intact, in date; do a fit check (cover and breathe in/out to check for leaks) every time it is put on.

    • Hard hat: shell not cracked, harness adjusted to fit, within expiry date, chin strap fitted when working at height.

  3. Defective PPE is not used. It is swapped from stock straight away and the damaged item handed to the Warehouse Manager.

  4. No PPE, no work. Anyone without the required PPE does not start the task until it is provided.

Stage 3 – Overhead work: hard hat zones

Hard hats are mandatory for everyone in a zone where work is going on overhead, where tools or materials could fall from above, or where there is a risk of striking the head on structures.

  1. Before overhead work starts (mobile towers, MEWPs, truss or rigging, ladders above head height, mezzanine loading, high racking), the crew chief sets up an overhead work zone below and around the work, using cones, barriers or tape, with a sign: "Overhead work in progress – hard hats must be worn".

  2. The zone extends far enough to catch anything that could fall or bounce: at least 2 m beyond the edge of the work platform, and more for high work or outdoors in wind.

  3. Everyone inside the zone wears a hard hat, including people passing through, the ground person for a MEWP, and people steadying a ladder. People working on the platform wear hard hats with chin straps fastened.

  4. Where possible, people are kept out of the zone altogether. Nobody stands directly below a person working at height or a suspended load.

  5. Tools are tethered and materials lifted in bags or by line, not thrown, to reduce the chance of things falling (see H5).

  6. At event sites, follow the venue's hard hat rules. Many venues require hard hats throughout the hall during build and break, whether or not overhead work is going on nearby.

  7. When overhead work finishes, the crew chief removes the zone and signage. Hard hats are no longer mandatory unless another overhead zone or venue rule applies.

Stage 4 – During work

  1. PPE is worn properly for the whole task: hi-vis fastened and not covered by other clothing; respirator kept on while dust or vapour is present (removing it even briefly removes the protection).

  2. If PPE is damaged during work, stop, move to a safe area and replace it.

  3. Supervisors check PPE use during the shift and correct anyone not wearing it.

Stage 5 – After use: cleaning, storage and replacement

  1. Reusable PPE is cleaned after use as the manufacturer advises, and stored dry, clean and out of direct sunlight. Respirators are stored in a sealed bag or box, away from contaminants. Hard hats are not left in vehicles in sunlight or near solvents.

  2. Disposable PPE (FFP3 masks, disposable gloves) is thrown away after the shift or when contaminated. Contaminated chemical gloves go into the correct waste bin as the COSHH sheet says.

  3. PPE is replaced when it meets the "replace when" conditions in the specification table, or at the manufacturer's expiry date. Replacement is free of charge.

  4. The Warehouse Manager checks PPE stock monthly, including sizes, filters and hard hat expiry dates, and re-orders before stocks run low.

Non-compliance

Situation Action
Person seen without required PPE Stop the task; person moves to a safe area and puts on the PPE before restarting
PPE not available (lost, damaged, out of stock) Task does not start or continue until PPE is provided; report to the Warehouse Manager
Repeated failure to wear PPE Recorded and dealt with by the Warehouse Manager or Managing Director under the company disciplinary procedure
Visitor or contractor refuses PPE Not allowed into the work area
PPE causes a problem (discomfort, skin reaction, poor fit, vision or hearing affected) Report it; an alternative is found. Do not remove PPE in a hazardous area without moving to safety first

Under the PPE at Work Regulations, employees and crew must use PPE in line with their training, look after it, and report its loss or defects. The company must provide it free of charge and make sure it is suitable.

Related documents

  • Premises Risk Assessment – Unit 1, Brickyard Road

  • H5 – Working at Height (overhead work zones, falling objects)

  • H8 – Manual Handling (gloves and safety footwear)

  • H19 – Fire

  • H21 – COSHH (chemical gloves, eye protection and RPE for each product)

  • SSOW-01 – Forklift Loading and Unloading

  • SSOW-02 – Lone Working

  • Product COSHH sheets and safety data sheets; face-fit test certificates

Action plan

Ref Action By whom Target date
Stock Check PPE stock covers all sizes, including wide-fit footwear and female-fit options Warehouse Manager Ongoing
P5 Arrange face-fit testing for all respirator wearers and keep certificates Warehouse Manager June 26
P6 Buy overhead work zone signs, cones and tape for the warehouse and event kit Warehouse Manager Ongoing
P6 Check hard hat manufacture dates and replace any past expiry Warehouse Manager Ongoing
Record Set up the PPE issue record and add PPE to the induction checklist Warehouse Manager Ongoing
All Brief all staff and crew on this SSOW and record signatures All Staff Ongoing

Sign-off
