documents.html:
Document details

This safe system of work sets out how Pickard Event Services staff use hand pallet trucks safely at Unit 1, Brickyard Road and on event sites: the checks before use, and how to pick up, move, steer, stop and set down loads. Pallet trucks are a key handling aid that reduce manual lifting (H8), but heavy loads moving on wheels bring their own risks of crushing, runaway loads and strain.

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
Reference SSOW-06 – Pallet Truck
Locations Unit 1, Brickyard Road (warehouse, loading area and yard), vehicle beds and tail lifts, and event sites (venue loading docks, halls and corridors)
Equipment Manual hand pallet trucks (hydraulic pump type), typically 2,000–2,500 kg rated capacity. Powered (electric) pedestrian pallet trucks are not covered here and need separate training and authorisation
Tasks Moving pallets, stillages, flight cases on pallets, staging and profile bundles around the warehouse; loading and unloading vans and trucks from the bed or tail lift; moving kit from venue loading docks to stands
Persons at risk Pallet truck users, people nearby, warehouse staff, venue staff and visitors
Assessor James Pickard
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner after an accident or near miss, new pallet trucks, or a change in how they are used

Key legislation and guidance: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999; Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER); Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 (pushing and pulling); Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992; HSE L23 (Manual handling – guidance on the regulations); HSE INDG478 (Risk assessment of pushing and pulling – RAPP tool); BS ISO 509 (pallet trucks – principal dimensions).

Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SSOW; provides suitable pallet trucks in good condition and enough for the work
Warehouse Manager Gives pallet truck training on induction; checks trucks are inspected and maintained; takes defective trucks out of use; stops unsafe use
Pallet truck users Have been trained; check the truck before use; follow this SSOW; report defects, damage and near misses
All staff, crew and visitors Keep clear of loads being moved; do not ride on pallet trucks; report hazards

Hazards and risk ratings

Risk = Likelihood (L) × Severity (S), each scored 1–5, as in the H-series risk assessments. Ratings are residual risk, with this SSOW followed. Runaway loads on slopes and tail lifts carry the highest residual risk (5, Medium); foot injuries and strains are the most frequent.

Score Likelihood Severity
1 Very unlikely Trivial – no treatment needed
2 Unlikely Minor – first aid only
3 Possible Moderate – medical treatment, up to 7 days off work
4 Likely Major – RIDDOR-reportable or over-7-day injury
5 Almost certain Fatal or permanent disability
Risk score Rating Action required
1–4 Low Maintain current controls; review annually
5–9 Medium Controls adequate but monitor; improve where reasonably practicable
10–16 High Further controls needed before or alongside work; management attention
20–25 Very high Stop work until risk is reduced
Ref Hazard Main controls (stage of this SSOW) Residual L × S Rating
PT1 Feet run over or crushed by wheels or forks Safety footwear; feet clear of wheels and forks; pull from the side (Stages 2, 3) 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
PT2 Runaway load on a slope, ramp or tail lift No slopes with heavy loads; two-person control; tail lift rules (Stage 4) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
PT3 Strain from pushing, pulling or starting heavy loads Within capacity; good condition wheels; get help; RAPP tool (Stages 1, 3) 2 × 2 = 4 Low
PT4 Load toppling or falling from the pallet Load stable, secured and centred; low speed; smooth floors (Stages 2, 3) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
PT5 Hands trapped between handle and objects, or under the load Hands on the handle grip only; clear route; never under a raised load (Stages 2, 3) 2 × 2 = 4 Low
PT6 Collision with people, racking or vehicles Clear route; push where you can see; walk, do not run; hi-vis (Stage 3) 1 × 3 = 3 Low
PT7 Trip hazard from a parked pallet truck Park forks lowered, handle upright, out of walkways (Stage 5) 2 × 2 = 4 Low
PT8 Overloading a vehicle bed, floor or tail lift Check capacities before loading (Stage 4) 1 × 4 = 4 Low

Before work starts

Training

  • Everyone who uses a pallet truck is shown how to use it safely on induction, covering this SSOW, and the training is recorded.

  • Users understand the truck's rated capacity, the three handle positions (lift, neutral, lower), steering, stopping, and the rules for slopes and tail lifts.

  • Powered pallet trucks may only be used by staff with specific training and authorisation.

Personal protective equipment

  • Safety footwear with toe caps at all times (SSOW-03).

  • Hi-vis in the warehouse, loading area and yard.

  • Gloves with good grip when handling pallets, straps or loads.

Pre-use check (user, each time before use)

Any defect = do not use. Tag the truck "Do not use" and tell the Warehouse Manager.

Area Check
Rated capacity Capacity label present and legible
Forks Not bent, cracked or twisted; both forks level
Wheels and rollers Steer wheels and fork rollers turn freely; no flat spots, chunks missing, cuts, or wrapped shrink-wrap or strapping
Handle and controls Handle not bent; control lever moves between lift, neutral and lower and works correctly; handle returns upright
Hydraulics Forks rise when pumped, hold height without creeping down, and lower smoothly; no oil leaks
Brake (if fitted) Parking or foot brake holds the truck
General No sharp edges or loose parts

Assess the move

Before moving a load, check:

  • Load weight: within the truck's rated capacity, and within what can be safely pushed and pulled on that floor. On a smooth, level floor one person can usually move up to about 1,000 kg; above that, or on rough floors, get help or use the forklift.

  • Load condition: stable, centred on the pallet, secured with shrink-wrap or straps if needed; pallet sound.

  • Route: clear, level and smooth, with no slopes, gaps, cables, kerbs, drains or debris, and wide enough for the load and turning.

  • Destination: has space to set the load down, and the floor or vehicle can take its weight.

Safe system of work – step by step

Stage 1 – Getting ready

  1. Complete the pre-use check and assess the move (above).

  2. Clear the route of obstructions. Make sure people nearby know a load is about to move.

  3. If the load is heavy, long or the route is difficult, get a second person or use the forklift (SSOW-05).

Stage 2 – Picking up the load

  1. Lower the forks fully: put the control lever in the lower position.

  2. Line the forks up square with the pallet openings, then push the forks fully into the pallet so the load sits over both forks, centred side to side. On a closed-bottom pallet, make sure the fork rollers will not land on a bottom board.

  3. Keep feet clear of the forks and wheels as you push in.

  4. Put the control lever in the lift position and pump the handle with smooth, full strokes until the pallet is just clear of the floor (about 25–50 mm). Do not lift higher than needed.

  5. Return the lever to neutral to travel.

  6. Check the load is stable and has not shifted. If it leans or moves, lower it and re-secure it.

Stage 3 – Moving the load

  1. Push the truck where possible, with the load in front, as pushing is easier on the body and gives you better control. On longer moves, or to turn in tight spaces, pull the truck from the side of the handle, never walking backwards in front of it.

  2. Keep both hands on the handle grip. Keep your body upright and use your legs and body weight to start the load moving, not your back.

  3. Walk, never run. Start, turn and stop gently. Heavy loads take longer to stop, so allow distance.

  4. Make sure you can see where you are going. If the load blocks your view, use a second person to guide you.

  5. Keep your feet away from the wheels and the forks, and keep a clear space between you and the load.

  6. Watch for people, corners, doorways, racking, columns, cables and uneven floor. Slow down at doorways and crossing points, and use walkways (SSOW-04).

  7. Do not let anyone ride on the truck or the load.

  8. Steer slowly; turning a heavy load sharply can tip it.

Stage 4 – Slopes, ramps, vehicle beds and tail lifts

  1. Avoid slopes and ramps with heavy loads. Manual pallet trucks have no effective brakes on a slope, and a loaded truck can run away.

  2. Where a slight slope cannot be avoided and the load is light: use two people, one controlling from the uphill side. Go straight up or down, never across. Never stand downhill of the load.

  3. Do not use a pallet truck on a steep ramp. Use the forklift, or split the load.

  4. Vehicle beds: check the vehicle's bed can take the weight and the vehicle is braked with the engine off (SSOW-01). Watch for gaps, the edge of the bed, and the curtain-side rails. Do not go near the open edge of the bed.

  5. Tail lifts: check the load plus the truck is within the tail lift's safe working load. Centre the load on the platform, lower the forks fully so the pallet sits on the platform, apply the pallet truck brake if fitted, and make sure the tail lift's roll-stops or safety barriers are up. Nobody stands on the tail lift with a heavy load; operate the tail lift from the side, clear of the load, and keep everyone away from under and around the platform.

  6. At venue loading docks, follow the venue's rules and check dock leveller plates are in place and secure before crossing.

Stage 5 – Setting down and parking

  1. Stop squarely at the set-down point, with feet clear.

  2. Put the control lever in the lower position and lower the load fully to the floor.

  3. Pull the forks straight out of the pallet. Do not drag the pallet.

  4. Check the load is stable and not blocking walkways, fire exits or fire equipment.

  5. Park the pallet truck in its designated place, out of walkways, with the forks fully lowered and the handle upright in the lock position, so it is not a trip hazard and cannot roll or swing.

  6. Clear any shrink-wrap, strapping or debris from the wheels, and report any defect.

Never

  • Never overload the pallet truck, or move a load you cannot control.

  • Never ride on the pallet truck or the load, or let anyone else do so.

  • Never use a pallet truck on a steep slope or ramp, or stand downhill of a loaded truck.

  • Never put your feet, hands or any part of your body under a raised pallet.

  • Never pull the truck walking backwards in front of the load.

  • Never use the pallet truck to lift people, or as a jack or a step.

  • Never use a defective pallet truck.

  • Never leave the truck with the forks raised, or with the handle down across a walkway.

  • Never stand on a tail lift with a heavy load.

Emergencies

Situation Action
Load starts to run away on a slope Do not try to stop it with your body or feet. Let go, step to the side out of its path, and shout a warning
Load starts to topple Step away; do not try to catch it; warn others
Foot or hand trapped or crushed Stop; release the load by lowering the forks if safe; call a first aider; 999 for serious injury
Load falls from a tail lift or vehicle Keep everyone clear; do not try to catch it; stop the tail lift; report
Fire alarm Lower the load, leave the truck clear of exits and walkways, evacuate (H19)

All accidents, near misses and damage are reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day and recorded; RIDDOR-reportable incidents are reported to HSE by the Managing Director.

Maintenance and inspection

Item Frequency By whom Record
Pre-use check Each use User Defects reported to the Warehouse Manager
Inspection: wheels, rollers, forks, hydraulics, handle Every 6 months Warehouse Manager or competent person Equipment register
Service and repair As needed, and as manufacturer recommends Competent person Equipment register

Each pallet truck has an ID number in the equipment register. Defective trucks are tagged and taken out of use until repaired or replaced.

Related documents

  • Premises Risk Assessment – Unit 1, Brickyard Road (W6 Manual handling)

  • H8 – Manual Handling (H8.6 Pushing and pulling)

  • SSOW-01 – Forklift Loading and Unloading

  • SSOW-03 – Personal Protective Equipment

  • SSOW-04 – Warehouse Operations

  • SSOW-05 – Forklift Operation

Action plan

Ref Action By whom Target date

Inspection Set up 6-monthly inspections of all pallet trucks Warehouse Manager Ongoing
PT2 Check the yard and venue loading routes for slopes; mark any slopes where loaded pallet trucks must not be used Warehouse Manager Ongoing
PT7 Mark a pallet truck parking area out of walkways Warehouse Manager Ongoing
Training Add pallet truck use to the induction checklist and record training Warehouse Manager Ongoing

Document control

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
SOP reference SOP-06 – Pallet Truck
Linked SSOW SSOW-06 – Pallet Truck
Version 1.0
Prepared by James Pickard (Managing Director)
Approved by Mathew Pickard (Director)
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner if SSOW-06 changes, after an accident or near miss, or when the equipment or task changes

1. Purpose

This SOP sets out the standard method for using a manual hand pallet truck at Pickard Event Services, so that every user checks, loads, moves, sets down and parks the truck the same way every time. It turns the controls in SSOW-06 – Pallet Truck into step-by-step instructions for use on the job. The hazards, risk ratings and controls are set out in SSOW-06, which must be read with this SOP.

2. Scope

This SOP covers the use of manual hand pallet trucks (hydraulic pump type, typically 2,000–2,500 kg rated capacity) to move loads around the warehouse, on and off vehicles and on event sites.

Applies to:

  • All staff and crew who use a pallet truck, and anyone acting as a second person or guide.
  • Unit 1, Brickyard Road (warehouse, loading area and yard), vehicle beds and tail lifts, and event sites (venue loading docks, halls and corridors).
  • Moving pallets, stillages, flight cases, staging and profile bundles; loading and unloading vans and trucks from the bed or tail lift; moving kit from venue loading docks to stands.

Does not cover:

  • Powered (electric) pedestrian pallet trucks, which need separate training and authorisation.
  • Forklift use, including moving loads too heavy or on routes too steep for a pallet truck (see SOP-05 and SSOW-05 – Forklift Operation).
  • Forklift loading and unloading of vehicles (see SOP-01 and SSOW-01 – Forklift Loading and Unloading).

3. Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves SSOW-06 and this SOP; provides suitable pallet trucks in good condition and enough for the work; reports RIDDOR-reportable incidents to HSE
Warehouse Manager Gives pallet truck training on induction and records it; makes sure trucks are inspected and maintained; takes defective trucks out of use; stops unsafe use; receives reports of defects, accidents and near misses
Pallet truck users Use a truck only once trained; carry out the pre-use check each time; assess each move; follow this SOP; report defects, damage and near misses
Second person (where used) Guides the user when the view is blocked, or helps control heavy loads and light loads on slight slopes from the uphill side
All staff, crew and visitors Keep clear of loads being moved; do not ride on pallet trucks; report hazards

4. Definitions

Term Meaning
Hand pallet truck Manual, hydraulic pump type truck used to lift a pallet just clear of the floor and move it by pushing or pulling
Rated capacity The maximum load the pallet truck is designed to carry, shown on its capacity label
Control lever positions Lift (pumping raises the forks), neutral (forks hold height for travel) and lower (forks come down)
Fork rollers The small load wheels at the tips of the forks
Safe working load The maximum load a tail lift is rated to carry, including the pallet truck
Roll-stops The safety barriers on a tail lift platform that stop a load rolling off
RAPP tool HSE tool (INDG478) for assessing the risk of pushing and pulling
Dock leveller plate The plate bridging the gap between a venue loading dock and a vehicle

5. Competence and authorisation

  • Only staff and crew who have been shown how to use a pallet truck safely on induction, covering SSOW-06, may use one. The training is recorded.
  • Users must understand the truck’s rated capacity, the three handle positions (lift, neutral, lower), steering, stopping, and the rules for slopes and tail lifts.
  • Powered pallet trucks may only be used by staff with specific training and authorisation. This SOP does not authorise their use.
  • All staff and crew are briefed on SSOW-06 and sign the briefing record; users also sign the acknowledgement record at the end of this SOP.

6. Equipment, PPE and materials

Item Requirement
Hand pallet truck Has an ID number in the equipment register and a legible capacity label; passes the pre-use check
Safety footwear Toe-capped safety footwear worn at all times (SSOW-03)
Hi-vis Worn in the warehouse, loading area and yard
Gloves Gloves with good grip when handling pallets, straps or loads
Shrink-wrap or straps Used to secure the load to the pallet where needed
“Do not use” tag Fitted to any truck found defective

7. Procedure

Follow these steps in order for every pallet truck move. The hazards behind each step are explained in SSOW-06.

7.1 Pre-use check

  1. Check the capacity label. Confirm the rated capacity label is present and legible.
  2. Check the forks. Forks must not be bent, cracked or twisted, and both must sit level.
  3. Check the wheels and rollers. Steer wheels and fork rollers must turn freely, with no flat spots, chunks missing, cuts, or wrapped shrink-wrap or strapping.
  4. Check the handle and controls. The handle must not be bent; the control lever must move between lift, neutral and lower and work correctly; the handle must return upright.
  5. Check the hydraulics. Pump the forks up: they must rise, hold height without creeping down, and lower smoothly, with no oil leaks.
  6. Check the brake, if fitted. The parking or foot brake must hold the truck.
  7. Check the general condition. Look for sharp edges or loose parts.
  8. Deal with any defect. If any check fails, do not use the truck. Tag it “Do not use” and tell the Warehouse Manager.

Hold point: Do not use the pallet truck until every pre-use check is passed. A truck with any defect stays tagged and out of use until repaired or replaced.

7.2 Assess the move and get ready

  1. Check the load weight. The load must be within the truck’s rated capacity and within what can safely be pushed and pulled on that floor. On a smooth, level floor one person can usually move up to about 1,000 kg; above that, or on rough floors, get help or use the forklift.
  2. Check the load condition. The load must be stable, centred on the pallet and secured with shrink-wrap or straps if needed, and the pallet must be sound.
  3. Check the route. The route must be clear, level and smooth, with no slopes, gaps, cables, kerbs, drains or debris, and wide enough for the load and for turning.
  4. Check the destination. There must be space to set the load down, and the floor or vehicle must be able to take its weight.
  5. Clear the route and warn others. Remove obstructions and make sure people nearby know a load is about to move.
  6. Get help if needed. If the load is heavy or long, or the route is difficult, get a second person or use the forklift (SSOW-05).

7.3 Pick up the load

  1. Lower the forks fully. Put the control lever in the lower position.
  2. Line up and enter the pallet. Line the forks up square with the pallet openings, then push them fully in so the load sits over both forks, centred side to side. On a closed-bottom pallet, make sure the fork rollers will not land on a bottom board.
  3. Keep feet clear. Keep your feet away from the forks and wheels as you push in.
  4. Lift the load. Put the lever in the lift position and pump the handle with smooth, full strokes until the pallet is just clear of the floor (about 25–50 mm). Do not lift higher than needed.
  5. Set the lever to neutral. Return the lever to neutral to travel.
  6. Check the load. Confirm the load is stable and has not shifted. If it leans or moves, lower it and re-secure it.

Hold point: Do not move off until the load is lifted only 25–50 mm, the lever is in neutral and the load is stable and secure.

7.4 Move the load

  1. Push where possible. Push the truck with the load in front. On longer moves, or to turn in tight spaces, pull from the side of the handle; never walk backwards in front of the truck.
  2. Use good posture. Keep both hands on the handle grip and your body upright, and use your legs and body weight, not your back, to start the load moving.
  3. Walk, never run. Start, turn and stop gently, and allow extra distance to stop heavy loads.
  4. Keep a clear view. If the load blocks your view, use a second person to guide you.
  5. Keep your body clear. Keep your feet away from the wheels and forks, and keep a clear space between you and the load.
  6. Watch the route. Look out for people, corners, doorways, racking, columns, cables and uneven floor. Slow down at doorways and crossing points, and use walkways (SSOW-04).
  7. No riders. Do not let anyone ride on the truck or the load.
  8. Steer slowly. Turning a heavy load sharply can tip it.

7.5 Slopes, ramps, vehicle beds and tail lifts

  1. Avoid slopes and ramps with heavy loads. Manual pallet trucks have no effective brakes on a slope and a loaded truck can run away.
  2. Control unavoidable slight slopes. Only with a light load: use two people, one controlling from the uphill side, go straight up or down, never across, and never stand downhill of the load.
  3. Do not use steep ramps. Use the forklift or split the load.
  4. Check vehicle beds. Confirm the bed can take the weight and the vehicle is braked with the engine off (SSOW-01). Watch for gaps, the edge of the bed and curtain-side rails, and do not go near the open edge of the bed.
  5. Check the tail lift load. Confirm the load plus the truck is within the tail lift’s safe working load.
  6. Set the load on the tail lift. Centre the load on the platform, lower the forks fully so the pallet sits on the platform, apply the pallet truck brake if fitted, and make sure the roll-stops or safety barriers are up.
  7. Operate the tail lift from the side. Nobody stands on the tail lift with a heavy load. Stay clear of the load and keep everyone away from under and around the platform.
  8. Follow venue dock rules. At venue loading docks, follow the venue’s rules and check dock leveller plates are in place and secure before crossing.

Hold point: Do not move a load onto a slope, vehicle bed or tail lift until the weight has been checked against the bed or tail lift capacity and, on a slope, two people are in place with one on the uphill side.

Hold point: Do not operate the tail lift until the load is centred, the forks are fully lowered, the brake (if fitted) is on, the roll-stops or barriers are up, and nobody is on, under or around the platform.

7.6 Set down and park

  1. Stop squarely. Stop at the set-down point, with your feet clear.
  2. Lower the load. Put the lever in the lower position and lower the load fully to the floor.
  3. Withdraw the forks. Pull the forks straight out of the pallet. Do not drag the pallet.
  4. Check the set-down. The load must be stable and must not block walkways, fire exits or fire equipment.
  5. Park the truck. Park in the designated place, out of walkways, with the forks fully lowered and the handle upright in the lock position so it cannot roll or swing.
  6. Clean and report. Clear any shrink-wrap, strapping or debris from the wheels, and report any defect to the Warehouse Manager.

8. Completion checks

Check Standard
Load position Load fully lowered, stable and at the intended set-down point
Access and exits No walkways, fire exits or fire equipment blocked
Pallet truck parked In its designated place, out of walkways, forks fully lowered, handle upright and locked
Wheels and rollers Clear of shrink-wrap, strapping and debris
Defects Any defect tagged “Do not use” and reported to the Warehouse Manager
Incidents Any accident, near miss or damage reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day

9. If something goes wrong

Situation Action
Load starts to run away on a slope Do not try to stop it with your body or feet. Let go, step to the side out of its path and shout a warning
Load starts to topple Step away; do not try to catch it; warn others
Foot or hand trapped or crushed Stop; lower the forks to release the load if safe; call a first aider; call 999 for serious injury
Load falls from a tail lift or vehicle Keep everyone clear; do not try to catch it; stop the tail lift; report it
Fire alarm Lower the load, leave the truck clear of exits and walkways, and evacuate (H19)
Accident, near miss or damage Report to the Warehouse Manager the same day so it is recorded; the Managing Director reports RIDDOR-reportable incidents to HSE

For the full emergency arrangements, refer to SSOW-06 – Pallet Truck.

10. Records

Record Completed by Kept by
Induction training record (pallet truck use) Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
Pre-use check defects User (reported each use) Warehouse Manager
6-monthly inspection (wheels, rollers, forks, hydraulics, handle) Warehouse Manager or competent person Equipment register
Service and repair (as needed and as manufacturer recommends) Competent person Equipment register
Pallet truck ID number and capacity Warehouse Manager Equipment register
Accident, near miss and damage reports Person involved, same day Warehouse Manager
SSOW-06 briefing and SOP acknowledgement Staff and crew Warehouse Manager

documents.html:
Document details

This safe system of work sets out how Pickard Event Services drivers drive company trucks safely and legally: who may drive, the checks before every journey, drivers’ hours, load security, driving, reversing and arriving at event sites. Loading and unloading by forklift at Unit 1 is covered in SSOW-01.

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
Reference SSOW-07 – Truck Driving
Vehicles Company curtain-side rigid trucks (over 3.5 tonnes, Category C1 or C), and any vans or hire vehicles used for event deliveries
Routes and locations Unit 1, Brickyard Road; public roads; client venues, exhibition halls, outdoor and event sites
Tasks Daily vehicle checks; planning journeys; driving loaded and unloaded; reversing and manoeuvring; arriving at, parking and leaving sites; securing loads; refuelling
Persons at risk Drivers, co-drivers and crew, other road users, pedestrians, staff and the public at Unit 1 and event sites
Assessor James Pickard
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner after a road traffic collision or near miss, a DVSA or police finding, a change in law, or new vehicles

Key legislation and guidance: Road Traffic Act 1988; Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986; Goods Vehicles (Licensing of Operators) Act 1995 (operator’s licence for goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes); assimilated EU/GB drivers’ hours rules (Regulation (EC) 561/2006) and tachograph rules; GB domestic drivers’ hours rules (Transport Act 1968) where they apply; Road Transport (Working Time) Regulations 2005; Vehicle Drivers (Certificates of Professional Competence) Regulations 2007; Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999; HSE INDG382 (Driving at work); DVSA Guide to maintaining roadworthiness; DVSA Securing loads on HGVs and goods vehicles; DVSA guide to drivers’ hours and tachographs; The Highway Code.

Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SSOW; holds or names the transport manager on the operator’s licence; makes sure vehicles are maintained, inspected and insured; plans work so drivers can keep within the hours rules
Transport manager (named on the O-licence) Continuous and effective management of the vehicles and drivers: licence checks, drivers’ hours and tachograph records, maintenance and safety inspections, defect reporting
Warehouse Manager Plans loads within vehicle weights; makes sure loads are secured before departure; supervises loading (SSOW-01)
Drivers Hold the correct, valid licence and Driver CPC; are fit to drive; complete the daily walkaround check; keep to the drivers’ hours rules and use the tachograph correctly; drive safely and legally; report defects, collisions and near misses
Co-drivers and banksmen Help with checks and load security; guide reversing from a safe position

Hazards and risk ratings

Risk = Likelihood (L) × Severity (S), each scored 1–5, as in the H-series risk assessments. Ratings are residual risk, with this SSOW followed. Road traffic collisions, driver fatigue and reversing carry the highest residual risk (5–6, Medium) because the outcome could be fatal to the driver or others.

Score Likelihood Severity
1 Very unlikely Trivial – no treatment needed
2 Unlikely Minor – first aid only
3 Possible Moderate – medical treatment, up to 7 days off work
4 Likely Major – RIDDOR-reportable or over-7-day injury
5 Almost certain Fatal or permanent disability
Risk score Rating Action required
1–4 Low Maintain current controls; review annually
5–9 Medium Controls adequate but monitor; improve where reasonably practicable
10–16 High Further controls needed before or alongside work; management attention
20–25 Very high Stop work until risk is reduced
Ref Hazard Main controls (section of this SSOW) Residual L × S Rating
TD1 Road traffic collision Licensed, CPC-trained drivers; safe driving rules; maintained vehicles (Before driving, Stage 2) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
TD2 Driver fatigue (early starts, late breaks, long event days) Drivers’ hours rules; journey planning; rest; fatigue reporting (Before driving) 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
TD3 Reversing into people or objects Avoid reversing; banksman; cameras and sensors; walk round first (Stage 3) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
TD4 Load shifting or falling in transit Load restraint to DVSA guidance; pre-departure check; re-check after first miles (Stage 1) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
TD5 Overloading (gross or axle weight) Load planning; known weights; weighbridge if in doubt (Stage 1) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
TD6 Bridge strike or low structure Vehicle height displayed in cab; route planning; HGV sat nav (Before driving, Stage 2) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
TD7 Vehicle defect (brakes, tyres, lights, steering) Daily walkaround check; safety inspections; defect reporting (Before driving) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
TD8 Falls from the cab or trailer bed Three points of contact; use steps; never jump down (Stage 5) 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
TD9 Distraction (phones, sat nav) Hands-free only; set route before driving; no phone use while driving (Stage 2) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
TD10 Pedestrians and other vehicles at busy event sites Site rules; walking pace; banksman; hazard lights (Stage 4) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
TD11 Breakdown or collision on the road Warning triangle; hi-vis; get out on the verge side; breakdown cover (Breakdowns section) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium

Before driving

Licence, Driver CPC and authorisation

  • Only drivers authorised by the Managing Director or transport manager may drive company trucks.
  • Drivers hold a valid licence for the vehicle category: C1 for rigid vehicles 3.5–7.5 tonnes; C for rigid vehicles over 7.5 tonnes. Licences are checked with the DVLA on authorisation and at least every 6 months, including endorsements.
  • Drivers of vehicles over 3.5 tonnes hold a valid Driver CPC (Driver Qualification Card), renewed by 35 hours of periodic training every 5 years.
  • Drivers hold a digital tachograph driver card and are trained in using the tachograph.
  • New drivers have a company induction and an assessed drive before driving alone.
  • Drivers tell the company straight away about any licence endorsement, disqualification, or medical condition that must be reported to the DVLA.

Fitness to drive

  • Drivers must not drive if they are unwell, overtired, or affected by alcohol, drugs or medication that can affect driving. The legal drink-drive limit in England and Wales is 80 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood (50 mg in Scotland); the company expects drivers to be completely free of alcohol when driving.
  • Group 2 (HGV) licence holders keep up to date with DVLA medical requirements, including medical reports at age 45 and then every 5 years.
  • Drivers who feel tired before or during a journey say so. Work plans are changed; nobody is expected to drive tired.

Drivers’ hours and tachograph

Company trucks over 3.5 tonnes are driven under the GB/EU drivers’ hours rules and must use a tachograph, unless the transport manager has confirmed an exemption applies.

Rule Limit
Daily driving 9 hours (may be 10 hours twice a week)
Break 45 minutes after no more than 4.5 hours’ driving (can be split as 15 minutes then 30 minutes)
Weekly driving 56 hours
Two-week driving 90 hours in any two consecutive weeks
Daily rest 11 hours (may be reduced to 9 hours no more than 3 times between weekly rests)
Weekly rest 45 hours (may be reduced to 24 hours, with compensation, under the rules)
Working time Average 48 hours a week; no more than 60 hours in any one week (Road Transport Working Time Regulations)
  • Insert the driver card at the start of the shift, record other work (loading, unloading, build and break) as other work, and record breaks and rest correctly.
  • Build and break work at events counts as work. Plan event days so that driving after long build or break shifts stays within the rules and does not cause fatigue.
  • Driver cards are downloaded at least every 28 days, and vehicle units at least every 90 days. Records are checked by the transport manager and kept for at least 12 months.

Daily walkaround check (driver, before the first journey of the day)

The driver checks the vehicle using the DVSA walkaround check and records it on the defect report. Any defect that makes the vehicle unroadworthy = vehicle not used until repaired.

Area Check
Lights and indicators All working, clean, undamaged; including brake lights and marker lights
Tyres and wheels Tread depth at least 1 mm (legal minimum for HGVs), no cuts or bulges, correct pressure; wheel nuts secure (check indicators)
Brakes Air pressure builds up correctly, no air leaks; parking brake holds
Steering No excessive play
Mirrors, cameras and glass All present, clean, adjusted, undamaged; windscreen not cracked in the driver’s view
Wipers and washers Working; washer fluid topped up
Fluid levels and leaks Oil, coolant, AdBlue and fuel; no leaks under the vehicle
Body and curtains Curtains, straps, buckles, poles and rails undamaged; doors and tail lift secure
Load restraint equipment Enough ratchet straps, load bars and edge protectors, in good condition
Number plates and markings Clean and legible; rear markings and reflectors present
Height indicator Vehicle height (feet and inches, and metres) displayed in the cab
Safety equipment Warning triangle, hi-vis, fire extinguisher, first aid kit, spill kit, torch
Tachograph Working, with the correct time; printer roll available

Journey planning

  • Plan the route using an HGV-specific sat nav or route planner, checking for low bridges, weight and width limits, and restricted roads. Know your vehicle height.
  • Check venue access details beforehand: delivery times, loading dock or gate, booking reference, height limits, and venue vehicle rules.
  • Allow time for traffic, breaks and rest. Do not plan journeys that need speeding or skipping breaks to meet event deadlines.
  • Check weather and traffic reports before setting off.

Safe system of work – step by step

Stage 1 – Load, weight and security (before departure)

  1. The load is planned so the vehicle’s gross vehicle weight and axle weights are not exceeded. Heavy items are placed low and spread evenly over the axles; the load is not concentrated at the rear. If unsure of the weight, use a weighbridge.
  2. Loads are placed tight to the headboard and to each other, with gaps filled using load bars, dunnage or blocks.
  3. Every item or block of items is restrained to the DVSA load-securing guidance using rated ratchet straps, load bars and edge protectors. Curtains are not load restraint.
  4. Straps are checked for cuts, fraying and damaged ratchets; damaged straps are discarded.
  5. The driver checks the load before departure: secure, within weights, nothing loose, nothing on the roof, curtains and doors fully closed and fastened, tail lift stowed and locked.
  6. Re-check the load restraint after the first few miles and at each stop, as straps can loosen as the load settles.
  7. For unloading and loading at Unit 1, follow SSOW-01.

Stage 2 – Driving

  1. Adjust the seat, mirrors and cameras before setting off. Wear a seatbelt; make sure any passengers do too.
  2. Set the sat nav route before driving. Do not hold or use a hand-held phone while driving, including when stopped in traffic. Hands-free calls only if unavoidable, kept short. Pull over safely to make or take longer calls.
  3. Keep to speed limits for goods vehicles (for example, rigid vehicles over 7.5 tonnes: 50 mph on single carriageways, 60 mph on dual carriageways and 56 mph speed-limited on motorways in England and Wales), and drive to the conditions.
  4. Keep a safe following distance; double it in wet weather and increase it further in ice and snow.
  5. Watch for vulnerable road users: cyclists, pedestrians and motorcyclists, especially in blind spots when turning left and at junctions.
  6. Know your height. Check signs for low bridges and structures. If a height restriction is lower than or the same as your vehicle height, do not go under it: stop and find another route.
  7. Take breaks as required by the drivers’ hours rules, and stop sooner if you feel tired. If you feel sleepy, find a safe place to stop, take a 15-minute nap and/or a caffeine drink, and do not continue until alert.
  8. Do not drive in severe weather (snow, ice, high winds for high-sided vehicles, flooding) if it is unsafe; contact the Managing Director to re-plan.

Stage 3 – Reversing and manoeuvring

  1. Avoid reversing where possible, by planning routes and parking so you can drive forwards.
  2. Before reversing, get out and walk round the vehicle to check the area is clear and to spot hazards and pedestrians.
  3. Use a trained banksman whenever vision is restricted or pedestrians are nearby. The banksman stands in a safe place, visible in the driver’s mirror, never directly behind the vehicle.
  4. If the driver loses sight of the banksman, stop immediately.
  5. Reverse slowly, using mirrors, cameras and sensors, with the reversing alarm working.
  6. At sites where there is no banksman and the area is busy, do not reverse until one is available.

Stage 4 – Arriving at event sites and venues

  1. Report to the venue’s gatehouse, loading dock or traffic marshal and follow their instructions and site rules.
  2. Drive at walking pace on site, with dipped headlights and hazard lights on where the venue requires it.
  3. Park only where directed, on firm level ground, clear of fire routes, fire exits, hydrants and pedestrian routes.
  4. Apply the parking brake, switch off the engine, and remove the key before getting out.
  5. Wear hi-vis and safety footwear (and a hard hat where required) as soon as you leave the cab on site (SSOW-03).
  6. Follow the venue’s loading and unloading rules. Where Pickard crew unload by forklift or pallet truck, follow SSOW-01, SSOW-05 and SSOW-06.
  7. Open curtains with care, checking for loads that have shifted in transit.

Stage 5 – Getting in and out of the cab and onto the trailer bed

  1. Use the steps and grab handles with three points of contact, facing the vehicle. Never jump down from the cab or bed.
  2. Keep steps clean, dry and free of mud or ice.
  3. Avoid climbing onto the trailer bed. Where you must, use the steps, keep away from the open edge, and never go on the bed while a forklift is working that side (H5, SSOW-01).

Stage 6 – Refuelling and end of shift

  1. Refuel with the engine off, no smoking, and the phone not in use. Clean up any spills with the spill kit.
  2. At the end of the shift: park at Unit 1 in the designated area, parking brake on, engine off, keys returned to the secure key box, vehicle locked.
  3. Report any defects found during the day on the defect report, and tell the transport manager about any incidents, damage or near misses.
  4. Remove the driver card (or record end of shift correctly) and make sure all activities are recorded.

Never

  • Never drive without the correct licence, Driver CPC and a completed walkaround check.
  • Never drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or when tired.
  • Never hold or use a hand-held phone while driving.
  • Never exceed the drivers’ hours limits or falsify tachograph records.
  • Never overload the vehicle or drive with an unsecured load.
  • Never drive under a bridge or structure if you are not sure your vehicle will fit.
  • Never reverse without checking behind first; never reverse blind where people may be.
  • Never carry passengers who are not part of the job, or more passengers than there are seats with seatbelts.
  • Never jump down from the cab or trailer bed.
  • Never leave the engine running with the vehicle unattended.

Breakdowns and road traffic collisions

Situation Action
Breakdown on a motorway or fast road Move onto the hard shoulder or an emergency area if possible; hazard lights on; leave by the passenger (verge) side; stand behind the safety barrier, away from the vehicle; wear hi-vis; call the breakdown provider and the Managing Director. Do not place a warning triangle on a motorway
Breakdown on other roads Pull over safely; hazard lights on; place the warning triangle at least 45 m behind if safe; wear hi-vis; call the breakdown provider
Road traffic collision Stop; switch off; hazard lights on; check for injuries and call 999 if anyone is hurt, the road is blocked or there is a dispute; do not admit liability; exchange details; take photos; report to the Managing Director as soon as possible
Bridge strike Stop; call 999 and the railway or bridge owner (number on the bridge if shown); do not move the vehicle until told it is safe
Load shift or spill on the road Stop in a safe place; hazard lights on; do not open curtains if the load is leaning on them; call the Managing Director and, if the road is affected, 999
Vehicle fire Stop; switch off; get everyone out and away; call 999; only use the extinguisher if the fire is very small and safe to tackle

All collisions, near misses, bridge strikes, load incidents and vehicle damage are reported to the transport manager the same day and recorded. RIDDOR-reportable incidents at work sites are reported to HSE by the Managing Director.

Records

Record Frequency By whom Kept for

Defect repairs When repaired Transport manager / maintenance provider At least 15 months
Safety inspections At set intervals (typically every 6–10 weeks, as on the O-licence) Maintenance provider At least 15 months
Annual test (MOT) Annually DVSA test centre Current certificate
Tachograph driver card download At least every 28 days Transport manager At least 12 months
Tachograph vehicle unit download At least every 90 days Transport manager At least 12 months
Driving licence checks (DVLA) On authorisation and at least every 6 months Transport manager Current
Driver CPC Check expiry; 35 hours training every 5 years Transport manager Current

documents.html:
Document control

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
SOP reference SOP-07 – Truck Driving
Linked SSOW SSOW-07 – Truck Driving
Version 1.0
Prepared by James Pickard (Managing Director)
Approved by Mathew Pickard (Director)
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner if SSOW-07 changes, after an accident or near miss, or when the equipment or task changes

1. Purpose

This SOP sets out the standard method Pickard Event Services drivers use to drive company trucks safely and legally, every time and in the same way. The hazards, risk ratings and controls for this task are in SSOW-07 – Truck Driving, which must be read with this SOP.

2. Scope

This SOP applies to every truck journey, from the first check of the day to parking up at the end of the shift.

Applies to:

  • Drivers, co-drivers, crew and banksmen.
  • Company curtain-side rigid trucks (over 3.5 tonnes, Category C1 or C), and any vans or hire vehicles used for event deliveries.
  • Unit 1, Brickyard Road; public roads; client venues and event sites.
  • Vehicle checks, journey planning, driving, reversing, site arrival and parking, load securing and refuelling.

Does not cover:

  • Loading and unloading by forklift at Unit 1 (SOP-01 / SSOW-01).
  • Forklift and pallet truck use when Pickard crew unload at sites (SOP-05 / SSOW-05 and SOP-06 / SSOW-06).

3. Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Names the transport manager; keeps vehicles maintained, inspected and insured; plans work within the hours rules; re-plans when drivers report tiredness or unsafe weather
Transport manager (named on the O-licence) Licence checks, drivers’ hours and tachograph records, maintenance and safety inspections, defect reporting
Warehouse Manager Plans loads within vehicle weights; makes sure loads are secured before departure; supervises loading (SOP-01)
Drivers Stay licensed and fit to drive; complete the walkaround check; keep to the hours rules; drive safely and legally; report defects, collisions and near misses
Co-drivers and banksmen Help with checks and load security; guide reversing from a safe position

4. Definitions

Term Meaning
O-licence Operator’s licence for goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes
Driver CPC Driver Certificate of Professional Competence (Driver Qualification Card)
Driver card The driver’s digital tachograph card
Other work Tachograph record for loading, unloading, build and break
Walkaround check DVSA daily vehicle check, recorded on the defect report
Gross and axle weights Maximum legal weight of the loaded vehicle and on each axle
Banksman Trained person who guides a reversing vehicle
Load restraint Rated straps, load bars and edge protectors; curtains are not load restraint

5. Competence and authorisation

  • Only drivers authorised by the Managing Director or transport manager may drive company trucks.
  • Hold a valid licence: C1 for rigid vehicles 3.5–7.5 tonnes; C for over 7.5 tonnes. Licences are checked with the DVLA on authorisation and at least every 6 months.
  • Hold a valid Driver CPC, renewed by 35 hours of periodic training every 5 years.
  • Hold a tachograph driver card and be trained in using the tachograph.
  • New drivers complete a company induction and an assessed drive before driving alone.
  • Group 2 (HGV) licence holders keep up to date with DVLA medical requirements, including medical reports at age 45 and then every 5 years.
  • Tell the company straight away about any licence endorsement, disqualification, or medical condition that must be reported to the DVLA.
  • Banksmen must be trained before guiding a reversing vehicle.

6. Equipment, PPE and materials

Item Requirement
Truck Passed the daily walkaround check; reversing alarm, cameras and sensors working
Height indicator Vehicle height (feet and inches, and metres) displayed in the cab
Sat nav HGV-specific sat nav or route planner
Tachograph Working, correct time, printer roll available; driver card carried
Load restraint Enough rated ratchet straps, load bars and edge protectors in good condition; dunnage or blocks to fill gaps
Vehicle safety equipment Warning triangle, hi-vis, fire extinguisher, first aid kit, spill kit, torch
PPE on site Hi-vis and safety footwear, plus a hard hat where required (SOP-03 / SSOW-03)
Defect report Walkaround defect report book, completed daily
Phone Hands-free use only, and only if unavoidable

7. Procedure

Follow these steps in order for every working day. Hazards and controls behind each step are in SSOW-07.

7.1 Fitness, hours and journey planning

  1. Confirm you are fit to drive. Do not drive if unwell, overtired, or affected by alcohol, drugs or medication that can affect driving. The company expects you to be completely free of alcohol when driving.
  2. Check your hours. Make sure the planned day keeps within the drivers’ hours and working time limits in SSOW-07, counting build and break work at events as work.
  3. Plan the route. Use an HGV sat nav or route planner, checking for low bridges, weight and width limits and restricted roads. Know your vehicle height. Confirm venue delivery times, gate or dock, booking reference, height limits and vehicle rules.
  4. Allow enough time. Build in traffic, breaks and rest; check weather and traffic reports. Never plan for speeding or skipped breaks.

Hold point: If you are tired, unwell or the day cannot be done within the hours rules, do not drive. Tell the Managing Director so the work plan is changed.

7.2 Daily walkaround check

  1. Insert your driver card. Do this at the start of the shift and check the tachograph shows the correct time.
  2. Carry out and record the walkaround check. Before the first journey of the day, check every area listed in SSOW-07 using the DVSA walkaround check, including tyre tread of at least 1 mm and secure wheel nuts. Record it on the defect report.

Hold point: Any defect that makes the vehicle unroadworthy means the vehicle is not used until it has been repaired.

7.3 Load, weight and security

  1. Keep within weights. Do not exceed gross or axle weights. Heavy items go low, spread over the axles, not at the rear. If unsure, use a weighbridge.
  2. Load tight. Load tight to the headboard and each other, filling gaps with load bars, dunnage or blocks.
  3. Restrain every item. Secure every item or block of items to the DVSA load-securing guidance using rated ratchet straps, load bars and edge protectors. Curtains are not load restraint. Discard any strap with cuts, fraying or a damaged ratchet.
  4. Check before departure. Nothing loose or on the roof, curtains and doors fully closed and fastened, tail lift stowed and locked.

Hold point: Do not move off until the load is secured and the pre-departure check is complete.

7.4 Driving

  1. Set up the cab. Adjust the seat, mirrors and cameras. Wear a seatbelt and make sure any passengers do too. Carry only passengers who are part of the job, and no more than there are seats with seatbelts.
  2. Set the sat nav before moving. Never hold or use a hand-held phone while driving, even in stopped traffic. Hands-free only if unavoidable, kept short.
  3. Keep to goods vehicle speed limits. For example, rigid vehicles over 7.5 tonnes: 50 mph on single carriageways, 60 mph on dual carriageways and 56 mph speed-limited on motorways in England and Wales. Drive to the conditions.
  4. Keep your distance and look out. Double the following distance in the wet and more in ice and snow. Watch for cyclists, pedestrians and motorcyclists, especially in blind spots when turning left and at junctions.
  5. Check height restrictions. If a restriction is lower than or the same as your vehicle height, do not go under it: stop and find another route.
  6. Re-check the load. Check load restraint after the first few miles and at each stop, as straps loosen as the load settles.
  7. Take breaks. Take breaks as the hours rules require, and stop sooner if tired. If sleepy, stop safely, take a 15-minute nap and/or a caffeine drink, and wait until alert.
  8. Stop for severe weather. If snow, ice, high winds or flooding make driving unsafe, contact the Managing Director to re-plan.

Hold point: Never drive under a bridge or structure unless you are sure your vehicle will fit.

7.5 Reversing and manoeuvring

  1. Avoid reversing. Plan routes and parking so you can drive forwards wherever possible.
  2. Walk round first. Before reversing, get out and walk round the vehicle to check the area is clear and spot hazards and pedestrians.
  3. Use a banksman. Use a trained banksman whenever vision is restricted or pedestrians are nearby, standing visible in your mirror, never directly behind the vehicle.
  4. Reverse slowly. Use mirrors, cameras and sensors, with the reversing alarm working.

Hold point: If you lose sight of the banksman, stop immediately. Where a site is busy and no banksman is available, do not reverse until one is.

7.6 Arriving at event sites and venues

  1. Report in. Report to the gatehouse, loading dock or traffic marshal and follow site rules. Drive at walking pace, with dipped headlights and hazard lights where the venue requires it.
  2. Park safely. Park only where directed, on firm level ground, clear of fire routes, exits, hydrants and pedestrian routes.
  3. Secure the vehicle. Apply the parking brake, switch off the engine and remove the key before getting out. Never leave the engine running with the vehicle unattended.
  4. Put on PPE. Wear hi-vis and safety footwear, and a hard hat where required, as soon as you leave the cab (SOP-03).
  5. Open curtains with care. Check for loads that have shifted in transit.
  6. Follow unloading rules. Follow the venue’s loading and unloading rules. Where Pickard crew unload by forklift or pallet truck, follow SOP-01, SOP-05 and SOP-06.

7.7 Getting in and out of the cab and onto the trailer bed

  1. Use three points of contact. Use the steps and grab handles facing the vehicle. Never jump down from the cab or bed. Keep steps clean, dry and free of mud or ice.
  2. Avoid the trailer bed. If you must, use the steps, keep from the open edge, and never go on it while a forklift works that side (H5, SOP-01).

7.8 Refuelling and end of shift

  1. Refuel safely. Engine off, no smoking and phone not in use. Clean up any spills with the spill kit.
  2. Park up at Unit 1. Park in the designated area with the parking brake on and engine off, return the keys to the secure key box and lock the vehicle.
  3. Report defects and incidents. Record any defects found during the day on the defect report, and tell the transport manager about any incidents, damage or near misses.
  4. Close the tachograph record. Remove the driver card (or record end of shift correctly), with other work, breaks and rest all recorded.

8. Completion checks

Check Standard
Walkaround check Completed and recorded before the first journey
Load Within weights, restrained to DVSA guidance, re-checked en route
Hours Within the drivers’ hours rules; tachograph record accurate
Vehicle at end of shift Parked at Unit 1, brake on, engine off, locked, keys in the key box
Reports Defects, damage, incidents and near misses reported to the transport manager the same day

9. If something goes wrong

Situation Action
Breakdown on a motorway or fast road Hard shoulder or emergency area if possible; hazards on; leave by the verge side; wait behind the barrier in hi-vis; call the breakdown provider and Managing Director. No warning triangle on a motorway
Breakdown on other roads Pull over safely; hazards on; triangle at least 45 m behind if safe; hi-vis; call the breakdown provider
Road traffic collision Stop; switch off; hazards on; call 999 if anyone is hurt, the road is blocked or there is a dispute; do not admit liability; exchange details; take photos; report to the Managing Director
Bridge strike Stop; call 999 and the railway or bridge owner (number on the bridge if shown); do not move the vehicle until told it is safe
Load shift or spill on the road Stop safely; hazards on; do not open curtains if the load leans on them; call the Managing Director, and 999 if the road is affected
Vehicle fire Stop; switch off; get everyone out and away; call 999; use the extinguisher only on a very small fire that is safe to tackle

Report all collisions, near misses, bridge strikes, load incidents and vehicle damage to the transport manager the same day. RIDDOR-reportable incidents at work sites are reported to HSE by the Managing Director. See SSOW-07 for the full breakdown and collision arrangements.

10. Records

Record Completed by Kept by
Walkaround check and defect report (daily) Driver Transport manager, 15 months minimum
Defect repairs Transport manager / maintenance provider Transport manager, 15 months minimum
Safety inspections (typically every 6–10 weeks) Maintenance provider Transport manager, 15 months minimum

Driver card download (every 28 days or sooner) Transport manager Transport manager, 12 months minimum
Vehicle unit download (every 90 days or sooner) Transport manager Transport manager, 12 months minimum
DVLA licence checks (every 6 months or sooner) Transport manager Transport manager, current
Driver CPC expiry Transport manager Transport manager, current
Incident and near miss reports Driver Transport manager

documents.html:
Document details

This safe system of work sets out how Pickard Event Services staff drive company vans (up to 3.5 tonnes gross vehicle weight) safely and legally: who may drive, the checks before each journey, payload, load security, drivers’ hours, driving, reversing and arriving at event sites. Trucks over 3.5 tonnes are covered in SSOW-07.

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
Reference SSOW-08 – Van Driving
Vehicles Company and hired panel vans, Luton vans and tail-lift vans up to 3.5 tonnes gross vehicle weight (GVW), and staff’s own vehicles if used for work (grey fleet)
Routes and locations Unit 1, Brickyard Road; public roads; client venues, exhibition halls, outdoor and event sites
Tasks Daily vehicle checks; loading and securing loads; driving to and from sites; reversing and manoeuvring; parking at venues; refuelling or charging
Persons at risk Drivers and passengers, other road users, pedestrians, staff and the public at Unit 1 and event sites
Assessor James Pickard
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner after a collision or near miss, a change in law, or new vehicles

Key legislation and guidance: Road Traffic Act 1988; Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986; GB domestic drivers’ hours rules (Transport Act 1968) for goods vehicles up to 3.5 tonnes; Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999; HSE INDG382 (Driving at work); DVSA Securing loads on HGVs and goods vehicles (principles also apply to vans); DVSA guidance on van overloading; The Highway Code.

Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SSOW; makes sure vans are maintained, insured for business use and fit for the job; plans work so drivers are not driving tired
Warehouse Manager Authorises van drivers; checks licences; plans loads within payload; checks loads are secured before departure; keeps vehicle records
Van drivers Hold a valid licence; are fit to drive; complete the daily check; keep within payload and drivers’ hours; secure loads; drive safely and legally; report defects, collisions and near misses
Passengers and crew Wear seatbelts; help with load security and as banksman when reversing; do not distract the driver

Hazards and risk ratings

Risk = Likelihood (L) × Severity (S), each scored 1–5, as in the H-series risk assessments. Ratings are residual risk, with this SSOW followed. Overloading, fatigue after long event days and unsecured loads are the most common van risks; collisions and reversing carry the highest residual risk because the outcome could be fatal.

Score Likelihood Severity
1 Very unlikely Trivial – no treatment needed
2 Unlikely Minor – first aid only
3 Possible Moderate – medical treatment, up to 7 days off work
4 Likely Major – RIDDOR-reportable or over-7-day injury
5 Almost certain Fatal or permanent disability
Risk score Rating Action required
1–4 Low Maintain current controls; review annually
5–9 Medium Controls adequate but monitor; improve where reasonably practicable
10–16 High Further controls needed before or alongside work; management attention
20–25 Very high Stop work until risk is reduced
Ref Hazard Main controls (section of this SSOW) Residual L × S Rating
VD1 Road traffic collision Licensed, authorised drivers; safe driving rules; maintained vans (Before driving, Stage 2) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
VD2 Driver fatigue (early starts, long build and break days) Drivers’ hours limits; journey planning; rest; fatigue reporting (Before driving) 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
VD3 Overloading (GVW or axle weight) Know the payload; known item weights; weighbridge if in doubt (Before driving, Stage 1) 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
VD4 Load shifting into the cab or out of the doors Bulkhead; load restraint; heavy items low and forward (Stage 1) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
VD5 Reversing into people or objects Avoid reversing; banksman; cameras and sensors; walk round first (Stage 3) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
VD6 Low structures (car parks, barriers, venue entrances) Know the van height, especially Luton and high-roof vans (Before driving, Stage 2) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
VD7 Vehicle defect Daily check; servicing; defect reporting (Before driving) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
VD8 Distraction (phones, sat nav, passengers) No hand-held phone use; set route before driving (Stage 2) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
VD9 Manual handling and falls when loading Handling aids; tail lift rules; three points of contact (Stage 1, Stage 5) 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
VD10 Breakdown or collision on the road Hi-vis; warning triangle; leave by the verge side; breakdown cover (Breakdowns section) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium

Before driving

Licence and authorisation

  • Only drivers authorised by the Warehouse Manager or Managing Director may drive company or hired vans.
  • Drivers hold a full, valid category B licence, which covers vans up to 3.5 tonnes GVW. Licences are checked with the DVLA on authorisation and at least every 6 months, including endorsements.
  • New drivers, and anyone not used to large vans, have a familiarisation drive before driving alone.
  • Drivers tell the company straight away about any licence endorsement, disqualification, or medical condition that must be reported to the DVLA.
  • Staff using their own vehicle for work must have business-use insurance, a valid MOT and road tax, and show these to the Warehouse Manager each year.

Fitness to drive

  • Do not drive if unwell, overtired, or affected by alcohol, drugs or medication that can affect driving. The legal drink-drive limit in England and Wales is 80 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood (50 mg in Scotland); the company expects drivers to be completely free of alcohol when driving.
  • Drivers who feel tired before or during a journey say so. Work plans are changed; nobody is expected to drive tired.

Drivers’ hours

Vans up to 3.5 tonnes used for goods in Great Britain fall under the GB domestic drivers’ hours rules. A tachograph is not needed for domestic journeys.

Rule Limit
Daily driving No more than 10 hours
Daily duty No more than 11 hours on duty in any working day (does not apply on days with no more than 4 hours’ driving)
Company rule: breaks A 15-minute break at least every 2 hours of driving, and a 45-minute break after no more than 4.5 hours
Company rule: rest At least 11 hours between the end of one working day and the next driving shift
  • Build and break work at events counts as duty. Plan event days so that driving home after long build or break shifts stays within these limits.
  • On late or long journeys, use a second driver or an overnight stay rather than one tired driver.
  • International journeys in vans over 2.5 tonnes need an operator’s licence and, from July 2026, a tachograph. Check with the Managing Director before any trip outside Great Britain.

Daily vehicle check (driver, before the first journey of the day)

Any defect that makes the van unsafe or illegal = van not used until repaired. Record the check and any defects on the van check sheet.

Area Check
Lights and indicators All working, clean, undamaged
Tyres Tread at least 1.6 mm (legal minimum), no cuts or bulges, correct pressure for the load
Brakes Footbrake and handbrake work correctly
Mirrors, cameras and glass Present, clean and adjusted; windscreen not cracked in the driver’s view
Wipers and washers Working; washer fluid topped up
Fluid levels and leaks Oil, coolant, AdBlue and fuel (or charge for electric vans); no leaks
Body, doors and bulkhead Doors close and lock; bulkhead intact; tail lift (if fitted) working and stowed
Load restraint Load-lashing points intact; enough ratchet straps and load bars, in good condition
Height Van height known and shown in the cab for high-roof and Luton vans
Safety equipment Warning triangle, hi-vis, first aid kit, fire extinguisher, torch

Payload (know your limits)

Vans are easily overloaded. Payload = GVW (on the plate, usually inside the driver’s door) minus the van’s unladen weight, and it includes the driver, passengers, tools and fuel.

  • Know the payload of each van, and the weight of heavy items such as staging decks, flight cases and truss.
  • Spread the load evenly and do not overload either axle, even if the total is within GVW.
  • If unsure, use a weighbridge. An overloaded van brakes and steers worse, and overloading is an offence.

Journey planning

  • Plan the route, including any low bridges, height-restricted car parks and venue access.
  • Check venue delivery times, entrances and loading rules before setting off.
  • Allow time for traffic and breaks. Do not plan journeys that need speeding or skipping breaks to meet event deadlines.

Safe system of work – step by step

Stage 1 – Loading and securing the load

  1. Check the total load is within the van’s payload, including the driver, passengers and tools.
  2. Load heavy items first, low down and forward against the bulkhead, spread evenly over both axles. Lighter items go on top and behind.
  3. Pack the load tight, filling gaps with load bars, dunnage or softer items so nothing can slide.
  4. Restrain the load using ratchet straps attached to the van’s lashing points, and load bars where fitted. Long items (profile, truss, poles) are strapped so they cannot slide forward into the cab or out of the rear doors. Nothing is carried loose in the cab.
  5. Use trolleys, sack trucks and the tail lift (if fitted) for heavy items, and get help for team lifts (H8, SSOW-06). Stand clear of the tail lift edge and never ride on it with a load.
  6. Check doors are closed and locked, the tail lift is stowed, and nothing is on the roof unless it is on a proper roof rack and strapped down.
  7. Re-check straps after the first few miles and at each stop.

Stage 2 – Driving

  1. Adjust the seat and mirrors before setting off. Wear a seatbelt; passengers must too. Only carry as many passengers as there are seats with seatbelts.
  2. Set the sat nav before driving. Do not hold or use a hand-held phone while driving, including when stopped in traffic. Use hands-free only if unavoidable and keep calls short; pull over safely for longer calls.
  3. Keep to the speed limits for vans: 50 mph on single carriageways, 60 mph on dual carriageways and 70 mph on motorways (lower limits apply where signed), and drive to the conditions. A loaded van takes longer to stop and is less stable on bends.
  4. Keep a safe following distance; double it in the wet and increase it further in ice and snow.
  5. Watch for cyclists, pedestrians and motorcyclists, especially in blind spots and when turning left.
  6. Know your height, especially in high-roof and Luton vans. Check signs at car parks, barriers, bridges and venue entrances.
  7. Take breaks as set out above, and stop sooner if tired. If you feel sleepy, find a safe place to stop, take a 15-minute nap and/or a caffeine drink, and do not continue until alert.
  8. In high winds, take extra care in high-sided vans and Luton vans; slow down or delay the journey if unsafe.

Stage 3 – Reversing and manoeuvring

  1. Avoid reversing where possible; park so you can drive away forwards.
  2. Before reversing, get out and walk round the van to check the area is clear.
  3. Use a banksman (a crew member) when vision is restricted or people are nearby. The banksman stands where the driver can see them in the mirror, never directly behind the van. If the driver loses sight of the banksman, stop.
  4. Reverse slowly, using mirrors, cameras and sensors.

Stage 4 – Arriving at event sites and venues

  1. Report to the venue’s gatehouse or loading dock and follow their site rules.
  2. Drive at walking pace on site, with hazard lights on where the venue requires it.
  3. Park only where directed, clear of fire routes, fire exits and pedestrian routes. Handbrake on, engine off, key removed.
  4. Put on hi-vis and safety footwear (and a hard hat where required) before leaving the van on site (SSOW-03).
  5. Open rear doors carefully, standing to one side, in case the load has shifted.

Stage 5 – Getting in and out

  1. Use the steps and handles with three points of contact when climbing into the load area or Luton box. Do not jump down.
  2. Keep the load floor clear of loose straps and packaging.

Stage 6 – Refuelling and end of shift

  1. Refuel with the engine off, no smoking and the phone not in use. For electric vans, charge only with undamaged cables at suitable charge points.
  2. At the end of the shift, park in the designated place at Unit 1, lock the van, and return the keys to the secure key box.
  3. Report any defects, damage, incidents or near misses to the Warehouse Manager.
  4. Lone late drives: send an “arrived safely” message to your buddy (SSOW-02).

Never

  • Never drive without a valid licence, authorisation and a completed daily check.
  • Never drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or when tired.
  • Never hold or use a hand-held phone while driving.
  • Never overload the van or drive with an unsecured load.
  • Never carry loose items in the cab, or passengers in the load area.
  • Never drive under a barrier, bridge or structure if you are not sure the van will fit.
  • Never reverse without checking behind first.
  • Never leave the engine running with the van unattended.

Breakdowns and road traffic collisions

Situation Action
Breakdown on a motorway or fast road Move onto the hard shoulder or an emergency area if possible; hazard lights on; leave by the passenger (verge) side; stand behind the safety barrier, away from the van; wear hi-vis; call the breakdown provider and the Managing Director. Do not place a warning triangle on a motorway
Breakdown on other roads Pull over safely; hazard lights on; place the warning triangle at least 45 m behind if safe; wear hi-vis; call the breakdown provider
Road traffic collision Stop; switch off; hazard lights on; check for injuries and call 999 if anyone is hurt, the road is blocked or there is a dispute; do not admit liability; exchange details; take photos; report to the Managing Director as soon as possible
Load shift Stop in a safe place; open doors carefully, standing to one side; re-secure the load; if it cannot be made safe, call the Managing Director
Vehicle fire Stop; switch off; get everyone out and away; call 999; only use the extinguisher if the fire is very small and safe to tackle

All collisions, near misses, load incidents and vehicle damage are reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day and recorded.

Records

Record Frequency By whom
Daily van check sheet and defect reports Each day before use Driver
Servicing As manufacturer’s schedule Maintenance provider / Warehouse Manager
MOT Annually (from 3 years old) Approved test centre
Insurance and road tax On renewal Managing Director
Driving licence checks (DVLA) On authorisation and at least every 6 months Warehouse Manager
Grey fleet documents (insurance, MOT, tax) Annually Warehouse Manager
Van payloads and heights When a van is added Warehouse Manager

Related documents

  • H8 – Manual Handling (H8.1 Loading and unloading)
  • SSOW-02 – Lone Working (journeys and late drives)
  • SSOW-03 – Personal Protective Equipment
  • SSOW-06 – Pallet Truck (tail lifts)
  • SSOW-07 – Truck Driving (vehicles over 3.5 tonnes)

Action plan

VD3 Record the payload of each van and display it in the cab, with weights of common heavy items Warehouse Manager Ongoing
VD6 Display the height of each high-roof and Luton van in the cab Warehouse Manager Ongoing

VD7 Introduce the daily van check sheet Warehouse Manager Ongoing
Grey fleet Collect business insurance, MOT and tax details from anyone using their own vehicle for work Warehouse Manager Ongoing
