documents.html:
Document control

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
SOP reference SOP-08 – Van Driving
Linked SSOW SSOW-08 – Van Driving
Version 1.0
Prepared by James Pickard (Managing Director)
Approved by Mathew Pickard (Director)
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner if SSOW-08 changes, after an accident or near miss, or when the equipment or task changes

1. Purpose

This SOP sets out the standard method for driving company vans safely and legally, from the first check of the day to handing back the keys, so every driver works the same way every time. The hazards, risk ratings and controls for van driving are in SSOW-08 – Van Driving, which must be read with this SOP.

2. Scope

This SOP covers all work-related driving of vans up to 3.5 tonnes gross vehicle weight (GVW), including the daily check, loading and securing the load, driving, reversing, arriving at venues, refuelling or charging, and end of shift.

Applies to:

  • All van drivers authorised by the Warehouse Manager or Managing Director, and passengers and crew travelling with them.
  • Company and hired panel vans, Luton vans and tail-lift vans up to 3.5 tonnes GVW.
  • Staff’s own vehicles when used for work (grey fleet).
  • Unit 1, Brickyard Road, public roads, client venues, exhibition halls, outdoor and event sites.

Does not cover:

  • Trucks over 3.5 tonnes: see SOP-07 and SSOW-07 – Truck Driving.
  • Journeys outside Great Britain: check with the Managing Director before any such trip (operator’s licence and tachograph rules may apply).

3. Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SOP and SSOW-08; makes sure vans are maintained, insured for business use and fit for the job; plans work so drivers are not driving tired; receives reports of breakdowns and collisions
Warehouse Manager Authorises van drivers; checks licences with the DVLA; plans loads within payload; checks loads are secured before departure; keeps vehicle records; receives defect, incident and near miss reports
Van drivers Hold a valid licence; are fit to drive; complete the daily check; keep within payload and drivers’ hours; secure loads; drive safely and legally; report defects, collisions and near misses
Passengers and crew Wear seatbelts; help with load security; act as banksman when reversing; do not distract the driver

4. Definitions

Term Meaning
GVW Gross vehicle weight: the maximum the van may weigh fully loaded, shown on the plate, usually inside the driver’s door
Payload GVW minus the van’s unladen weight; it includes the driver, passengers, tools and fuel
Bulkhead The fixed partition between the cab and the load area
Lashing points Fixed anchor points in the load area for attaching ratchet straps
Banksman A crew member who guides the driver when reversing, standing where the driver can see them in the mirror
Grey fleet Staff’s own vehicles used for work
GB domestic drivers’ hours rules The legal driving and duty limits for goods vans up to 3.5 tonnes in Great Britain

5. Competence and authorisation

  • Only drivers authorised by the Warehouse Manager or Managing Director may drive company or hired vans.
  • Drivers must hold a full, valid category B licence, which covers vans up to 3.5 tonnes GVW.
  • Licences, including endorsements, are checked with the DVLA on authorisation and at least every 6 months.
  • New drivers, and anyone not used to large vans, have a familiarisation drive before driving alone.
  • Drivers must tell the company straight away about any licence endorsement, disqualification, or medical condition that must be reported to the DVLA.
  • Staff using their own vehicle for work must have business-use insurance, a valid MOT and road tax, and show these to the Warehouse Manager each year.
  • All van drivers are briefed on SSOW-08 and sign the driver authorisation and briefing record.

6. Equipment, PPE and materials

Item Requirement
Van check sheet Completed before the first journey of the day; defects recorded
Ratchet straps and load bars Enough for the load, in good condition, attached to the van’s lashing points
Dunnage or softer items Used to fill gaps so the load cannot slide
Trolleys, sack trucks, tail lift Used for heavy items; tail lift (if fitted) working and stowed
Warning triangle Carried in the van; not used on motorways
Hi-vis Carried in the van; worn at breakdowns and on site
First aid kit, fire extinguisher, torch Carried in the van and checked daily
Safety footwear and hard hat Safety footwear on site; hard hat where the venue requires it (SSOW-03)
Payload and height information Payload known for each van; height shown in the cab for high-roof and Luton vans

7. Procedure

Follow these steps in order for every working day that involves van driving.

7.1 Before driving

  1. Check you are fit to drive. Do not drive if unwell, overtired, or affected by alcohol, drugs or medication that can affect driving. The company expects drivers to be completely free of alcohol when driving; if you feel tired, say so and the work plan will be changed.
  2. Check your hours. Plan the day within the GB domestic drivers’ hours rules and company rules: no more than 10 hours’ driving and 11 hours on duty in a working day, a 15-minute break at least every 2 hours of driving, a 45-minute break after no more than 4.5 hours, and at least 11 hours’ rest before the next driving shift. Build and break work at events counts as duty.
  3. Plan the journey. Plan the route around low bridges and height-restricted car parks, and check venue delivery times, entrances and loading rules. Allow time for traffic and breaks; on late or long journeys use a second driver or an overnight stay.
  4. Complete the daily vehicle check. Before the first journey of the day, work through every area in the SSOW-08 daily check table, including tyres (tread at least 1.6 mm, no cuts or bulges, correct pressure for the load), brakes, lights, mirrors, bulkhead, load restraint and safety equipment.
  5. Record the check. Record the check and any defects on the van check sheet. Any defect that makes the van unsafe or illegal means the van is not used until repaired.

Hold point: Do not drive until you are authorised, fit to drive, within your hours, and the daily check is complete with no defect that makes the van unsafe or illegal.

7.2 Loading and securing the load

  1. Check the payload. Confirm the total load, including the driver, passengers and tools, is within the van’s payload. Know the weight of heavy items such as staging decks, flight cases and truss; if unsure, use a weighbridge.
  2. Load heavy items first. Place them low down and forward against the bulkhead, spread evenly over both axles so neither axle is overloaded. Put lighter items on top and behind.
  3. Pack the load tight. Fill gaps with load bars, dunnage or softer items so nothing can slide.
  4. Restrain the load. Use ratchet straps attached to the lashing points, and load bars where fitted. Strap long items (profile, truss, poles) so they cannot slide forward into the cab or out of the rear doors. Carry nothing loose in the cab.
  5. Use handling aids. Use trolleys, sack trucks and the tail lift (if fitted) for heavy items, and get help for team lifts (H8, SSOW-06). Stand clear of the tail lift edge and never ride on it with a load.
  6. Secure the van. Check doors are closed and locked and the tail lift is stowed. Nothing goes on the roof unless it is on a proper roof rack and strapped down.

Hold point: Do not set off until the load is within payload, restrained, and checked as secure by the Warehouse Manager before departure.

7.3 Driving

  1. Set up the cab. Adjust the seat and mirrors before setting off. Wear a seatbelt and make sure passengers do; carry only as many passengers as there are seats with seatbelts, and never in the load area.
  2. Set the sat nav before driving. Do not hold or use a hand-held phone while driving, including when stopped in traffic. Use hands-free only if unavoidable, keep calls short, and pull over safely for longer calls.
  3. Keep to van speed limits. Drive at no more than 50 mph on single carriageways, 60 mph on dual carriageways and 70 mph on motorways, or lower where signed, and drive to the conditions. A loaded van takes longer to stop and is less stable on bends.
  4. Keep your distance. Keep a safe following distance; double it in the wet and increase it further in ice and snow.
  5. Watch for vulnerable road users. Look for cyclists, pedestrians and motorcyclists, especially in blind spots and when turning left.
  6. Know your height. In high-roof and Luton vans especially, check signs at car parks, barriers, bridges and venue entrances. Never drive under a structure if you are not sure the van will fit.
  7. Re-check straps. Check the load restraint after the first few miles and at each stop.
  8. Take breaks and stop if tired. Take breaks as planned and stop sooner if tired. If you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place, take a 15-minute nap and/or a caffeine drink, and do not continue until alert.
  9. Take care in high winds. Take extra care in high-sided and Luton vans; slow down or delay the journey if unsafe.

7.4 Reversing and manoeuvring

  1. Avoid reversing. Where possible, park so you can drive away forwards.
  2. Walk round first. Before reversing, get out and walk round the van to check the area is clear.
  3. Use a banksman. Use a crew member as banksman when vision is restricted or people are nearby. The banksman stands where you can see them in the mirror, never directly behind the van.
  4. Reverse slowly. Use mirrors, cameras and sensors throughout.

Hold point: If you lose sight of the banksman, stop immediately and do not move until you can see them again.

7.5 Arriving at event sites and venues

  1. Report in. Report to the venue’s gatehouse or loading dock and follow their site rules.
  2. Drive at walking pace. Keep to walking pace on site, with hazard lights on where the venue requires it.
  3. Park where directed. Park only where directed, clear of fire routes, fire exits and pedestrian routes. Put the handbrake on, switch the engine off and remove the key; never leave the engine running with the van unattended.
  4. Put on PPE. Put on hi-vis and safety footwear, and a hard hat where required, before leaving the van on site (SSOW-03).
  5. Open rear doors carefully. Stand to one side when opening, in case the load has shifted.
  6. Get in and out safely. Use the steps and handles with three points of contact when climbing into the load area or Luton box. Do not jump down, and keep the load floor clear of loose straps and packaging.

7.6 Refuelling and end of shift

  1. Refuel or charge safely. Refuel with the engine off, no smoking and the phone not in use. For electric vans, charge only with undamaged cables at suitable charge points.
  2. Park and secure the van. At the end of the shift, park in the designated place at Unit 1, lock the van and return the keys to the secure key box.
  3. Report problems. Report any defects, damage, incidents or near misses to the Warehouse Manager the same day.
  4. Confirm safe arrival. After a lone late drive, send an “arrived safely” message to your buddy (SSOW-02).

8. Completion checks

Check Standard
Daily check Completed and recorded on the van check sheet before the first journey; no unsafe or illegal defect
Load Within payload, heavy items low and forward, restrained, nothing loose in the cab
Site parking Clear of fire routes, fire exits and pedestrian routes; handbrake on, engine off, key removed
Van at Unit 1 Parked in the designated place, locked, keys in the secure key box
Reporting Defects, damage, incidents and near misses reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day
Lone late drive “Arrived safely” message sent to buddy

9. If something goes wrong

Situation Action
Breakdown on a motorway or fast road Move to the hard shoulder or an emergency area if possible; hazard lights on; leave by the passenger (verge) side; stand behind the barrier, away from the van; wear hi-vis; call the breakdown provider and the Managing Director; no warning triangle on a motorway
Breakdown on other roads Pull over safely; hazard lights on; place the warning triangle at least 45 m behind if safe; wear hi-vis; call the breakdown provider
Road traffic collision Stop; switch off; hazard lights on; check for injuries; call 999 if anyone is hurt, the road is blocked or there is a dispute; do not admit liability; exchange details; take photos; report to the Managing Director as soon as possible
Load shift Stop in a safe place; open doors carefully, standing to one side; re-secure the load; if it cannot be made safe, call the Managing Director
Vehicle fire Stop; switch off; get everyone out and away; call 999; use the extinguisher only if the fire is very small and safe to tackle

Report all collisions, near misses, load incidents and vehicle damage to the Warehouse Manager the same day so they are recorded. See SSOW-08 for the full breakdown and collision arrangements.

10. Records

Record Completed by Kept by
Daily van check sheet and defect reports (each day before use) Driver Warehouse Manager
Servicing (to the manufacturer’s schedule) Maintenance provider Warehouse Manager
MOT (annually, from 3 years old) Approved test centre Warehouse Manager
Insurance and road tax (on renewal) Managing Director Managing Director
DVLA licence checks (on authorisation and at least every 6 months) Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
Grey fleet insurance, MOT and tax (annually) Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
Van payloads and heights (when a van is added) Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
Driver authorisation and briefing record Driver Warehouse Manager

documents.html:
Document details

This safe system of work sets out how Pickard Event Services staff use tail lifts on company trucks and vans safely: who may operate them, the checks before use, and how to deploy, load, raise, lower and stow the platform. Tail lifts are lifting equipment under LOLER, and the main dangers are falls from the platform, crushing of feet and hands, and loads rolling or toppling off the edge.

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
Reference SSOW-09 – Tail Lift Operation
Equipment Tail lifts fitted to company and hired trucks and vans (cantilever, column and slider types)
Locations Unit 1, Brickyard Road (loading area and yard) and event sites (venue loading docks, roads and car parks)
Tasks Deploying and stowing the platform; moving pallets, flight cases, roll cages and equipment on and off the platform with pallet trucks, sack trucks and dollies; raising and lowering loads between the ground and the vehicle bed
Persons at risk Tail lift operators, crew, drivers, venue staff, pedestrians and members of the public near the vehicle
Assessor James Pickard
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner after an accident or near miss, a new type of tail lift, or a change in how they are used

Key legislation and guidance: Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 (LOLER); Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER); Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999; Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992; Work at Height Regulations 2005; BS EN 1756-1 (Tail lifts – platform lifts for mounting on wheeled vehicles); Road Haulage Association and FTA/Logistics UK tail lift guidance; DVSA Guide to maintaining roadworthiness.

Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SSOW; makes sure tail lifts are maintained and have current LOLER thorough examinations
Warehouse Manager / transport manager Gives tail lift training; authorises operators; keeps LOLER and maintenance records; takes defective tail lifts out of use
Tail lift operators (drivers and crew) Have been trained on the type of tail lift; carry out pre-use checks; follow this SSOW; control the area around the platform; report defects and incidents
Other crew Stay clear of the platform and its area of movement unless directed by the operator

Hazards and risk ratings

Risk = Likelihood (L) × Severity (S), each scored 1–5, as in the H-series risk assessments. Ratings are residual risk, with this SSOW followed. Loads rolling off the platform and falls from the platform carry the highest residual risk (5–6, Medium); crushed feet are the most common tail lift injury.

Score Likelihood Severity
1 Very unlikely Trivial – no treatment needed
2 Unlikely Minor – first aid only
3 Possible Moderate – medical treatment, up to 7 days off work
4 Likely Major – RIDDOR-reportable or over-7-day injury
5 Almost certain Fatal or permanent disability
Risk score Rating Action required
1–4 Low Maintain current controls; review annually
5–9 Medium Controls adequate but monitor; improve where reasonably practicable
10–16 High Further controls needed before or alongside work; management attention
20–25 Very high Stop work until risk is reduced
Ref Hazard Main controls (stage of this SSOW) Residual L × S Rating
TL1 Wheeled load rolling off the platform Roll stops up; load centred; pallet truck brake or forks lowered; level ground (Stages 1, 2) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
TL2 Operator falling from the platform Stay inside the platform; handrails or guards where fitted; no riding with heavy loads; three points of contact (Stages 2, 3) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
TL3 Feet crushed under or between the platform and ground or vehicle Safety footwear; feet clear of the platform edge; hold-to-run controls (Stage 3) 2 × 3 = 6 Medium
TL4 Hands or fingers trapped in the mechanism or between load and vehicle Hands on the controls or handrail only; keep clear of hinges and arms (Stage 3) 1 × 3 = 3 Low
TL5 Overloading the platform Safe working load (SWL) and load centre marked and kept to (Stage 2) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
TL6 Load toppling from the platform Stable, secured loads; low centre of gravity; tall items strapped or held by two people (Stage 2) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
TL7 Pedestrians or vehicles struck by the platform or a falling load Exclusion zone; cones; nobody under or beside the platform (Stage 1) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
TL8 Tail lift failure (hydraulic, structural, electrical) Pre-use checks; maintenance; LOLER thorough examination every 6 months 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
TL9 Tail lift left deployed and struck while driving Stowed and locked before moving; warning light checked (Stage 4) 1 × 4 = 4 Low

Before use

Training and authorisation

  • Only staff trained on the type of tail lift fitted, and authorised by the Warehouse Manager, may operate it. Training covers this SSOW, the controls, the SWL and load centre, the emergency stop and the emergency lowering procedure.
  • Hired vehicles: the operator checks the controls and emergency stop on that specific tail lift before first use.

Personal protective equipment

  • Safety footwear with toe caps (SSOW-03).
  • Hi-vis, especially at the roadside and in loading areas.
  • Gloves with good grip for handling loads and straps.

Pre-use check (operator, before first use each day)

Any defect = tail lift not used. Isolate it, tag it “Do not use” and report it to the Warehouse Manager.

Area Check
SWL and markings Safe working load and load centre plate present and legible; LOLER examination date in date
Platform No cracks, bends or damage; surface anti-slip and free of oil, ice and debris
Roll stops and guards Roll stops (cart stops) raise and lower correctly; handrails or safety barriers (if fitted) secure
Controls All controls work and return to off when released (hold-to-run); two-handed or foot controls work as designed; emergency stop works
Hydraulics No leaks from hoses, rams or fittings; platform does not creep down when held in position
Structure Arms, hinges, pins and mounting bolts secure and undamaged
Warning devices Flashing lights or flags on the platform working; cab warning light works when deployed
Power Battery and isolator switch working

Site set-up

  1. Park on firm, level ground, with the handbrake on, engine off (unless the tail lift needs the engine running) and the key removed.
  2. Check there is enough space behind the vehicle for the platform to open and lower, and for the load to be moved off it, with no overhead obstructions.
  3. Avoid using the tail lift on a slope, on soft or uneven ground, or near kerbs, drains and potholes.
  4. Set up an exclusion zone behind the vehicle with cones or barriers, especially at the roadside or in public areas. Use the platform warning lights or flags.
  5. Check lighting is adequate for the work.

Safe system of work – step by step

Stage 1 – Deploying the platform

  1. Switch on the tail lift at the isolator or cab switch. Check the cab warning light comes on.
  2. Make sure nobody is behind the vehicle or within the platform’s area of movement.
  3. Release any locking catches or safety chains, standing to the side, never directly behind the platform.
  4. Open (unfold) the platform and lower it to the ground using the controls, watching it all the way down.
  5. Check the platform is lying flat and stable on the ground, and raise the roll stops (cart stops) where fitted.

Stage 2 – Loading the platform

  1. Check the load is within the platform’s SWL, and that its weight will be at or inside the marked load centre. Remember to include the weight of the pallet truck or trolley and the operator if they ride.
  2. Move the load onto the platform squarely and slowly, using a pallet truck, sack truck or dolly as needed. Centre it on the platform, away from the edges.
  3. Wheeled loads: lower the pallet truck forks fully so the load sits on the platform, apply the brake on cages or trolleys, and make sure the roll stops are up at the outer edge.
  4. Tall or unstable loads (stacked cases, panels, furniture): strap them together or have two people steady them from a safe position, never from below or in front.
  5. Only one load at a time unless the platform is designed for more and the total is within SWL.

Stage 3 – Raising and lowering

  1. Operate the tail lift only from the designated control position, with a clear view of the platform and load.
  2. Keep feet clear of the platform edge and away from underneath it. Keep hands on the controls or handrail, away from hinges and arms.
  3. Use the hold-to-run controls smoothly; stop at once if anything moves, shifts or looks wrong.
  4. Riding the platform: only where the tail lift is designed and marked for an operator to ride (with a marked standing position and, where fitted, handrails), standing within the marked area, facing the vehicle, holding the handrail, with feet well inside the edge. Never ride the platform with a heavy wheeled load that you could not hold if it moved; instead, operate from the ground.
  5. When the platform reaches bed level, check it is level with the vehicle bed before moving the load across. Lower the roll stops only when you are ready to move the load.
  6. Move the load into the vehicle and secure it straight away (SSOW-07, SSOW-08).
  7. When unloading, reverse the process: move the load onto the platform, raise the roll stops, apply brakes, lower to the ground, and move the load away before the platform is raised again.

Stage 4 – Stowing

  1. Clear the platform of loads, straps and debris.
  2. Lower the roll stops (if they fold away), raise the platform and fold or slide it into the stowed position.
  3. Fit the locking catches or safety chains, and check the platform is fully stowed and secure.
  4. Switch off the tail lift at the isolator or cab switch, and check the cab warning light is off before driving away.
  5. Remove the cones or barriers.

Never

  • Never operate a tail lift without training, authorisation and a pre-use check.
  • Never exceed the SWL, or place the load outside the load centre.
  • Never use the tail lift with the roll stops down when a wheeled load is on the platform.
  • Never stand, walk or put your feet under or beside a moving platform.
  • Never ride the platform unless it is designed for it, or with a heavy wheeled load.
  • Never let anyone else ride the platform, or use it to lift people other than the operator.
  • Never use the tail lift on a slope or soft ground.
  • Never leave the platform deployed and unattended in a public area.
  • Never drive with the tail lift unstowed or the warning light on.
  • Never use a defective tail lift or override a safety device.

Emergencies

Situation Action
Load starts to roll or topple Let go and step clear to the side; do not try to stop it with your body; shout a warning
Person trapped Press the emergency stop; call for help; if safe, use the controls or emergency lowering to free them; call 999 for any serious injury
Tail lift fails with a load raised Stop; keep everyone clear from under the platform; do not climb on it; use the emergency lowering procedure only if trained; otherwise call the maintenance provider
Platform will not stow Do not drive; make the area safe; call the maintenance provider

All accidents, near misses and defects are reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day and recorded; RIDDOR-reportable incidents (including dangerous occurrences such as the failure of lifting equipment) are reported to HSE by the Managing Director.

Inspection and records

Item Frequency By whom Record
Pre-use check Before first use each day Operator Vehicle check sheet
Service and maintenance As manufacturer’s schedule, and at vehicle safety inspections Competent engineer Service record
LOLER thorough examination At least every 6 months Competent person Report of thorough examination (kept at least 2 years or until the next report)
Operator training On induction; refresher every 3 years Warehouse Manager Training record

Document control

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
SOP reference SOP-09 – Tail Lift Operation
Linked SSOW SSOW-09 – Tail Lift Operation
Version 1.0
Prepared by James Pickard (Managing Director)
Approved by Mathew Pickard (Director)
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner if SSOW-09 changes, after an accident or near miss, or when the equipment or task changes

1. Purpose

This SOP sets out the standard method for operating tail lifts on company and hired trucks and vans, so that every operator checks, deploys, loads, raises, lowers and stows the platform the same way every time. Tail lifts are lifting equipment under LOLER. The hazards, risk ratings and controls for this task are in SSOW-09 – Tail Lift Operation, which must be read with this SOP.

2. Scope

This SOP covers the use of tail lifts by Pickard Event Services drivers and crew from the pre-use check through to stowing the platform and leaving the site.

Applies to:

  • Tail lift operators (drivers and crew) trained and authorised on the type of tail lift fitted, and other crew working near the vehicle.
  • Unit 1, Brickyard Road (loading area and yard) and event sites (venue loading docks, roads and car parks).
  • Tail lifts fitted to company and hired trucks and vans (cantilever, column and slider types).
  • Deploying and stowing the platform; moving pallets, flight cases, roll cages and equipment on and off the platform with pallet trucks, sack trucks and dollies; raising and lowering loads between the ground and the vehicle bed.

Does not cover:

  • Securing loads inside the vehicle and driving (SOP-07 Truck Driving / SSOW-07, SOP-08 Van Driving / SSOW-08).
  • General pallet truck operation (SOP-06 Pallet Truck / SSOW-06).
  • Manual handling assessment of loads (H8 – Manual Handling, H8.1 Loading and unloading).
  • Servicing, maintenance and LOLER thorough examination, which are carried out by a competent engineer or competent person.

3. Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves SSOW-09 and this SOP; makes sure tail lifts are maintained and have current LOLER thorough examinations; reports RIDDOR-reportable incidents to HSE
Warehouse Manager / transport manager Gives tail lift training; authorises operators; keeps LOLER and maintenance records; takes defective tail lifts out of use; receives defect and incident reports
Tail lift operators (drivers and crew) Operate only tail lift types they are trained on; carry out pre-use checks; follow this SOP and SSOW-09; control the area around the platform; report defects and incidents
Other crew Stay clear of the platform and its area of movement unless directed by the operator

4. Definitions

Term Meaning
SWL Safe working load: the maximum load the tail lift may lift, shown on the marked plate
Load centre The marked position on the platform within which the weight of the load must sit
Roll stops (cart stops) Flaps at the outer edge of the platform that stop wheeled loads rolling off
Hold-to-run controls Controls that only operate while held and return to off when released
Exclusion zone The area behind the vehicle, marked with cones or barriers, kept clear while the tail lift is in use
Emergency lowering The procedure for lowering the platform if the tail lift fails; used only by trained operators
LOLER thorough examination Statutory examination of the tail lift by a competent person, at least every 6 months

5. Competence and authorisation

  • Only staff trained on the type of tail lift fitted, and authorised by the Warehouse Manager, may operate it.
  • Training covers SSOW-09, the controls, the SWL and load centre, the emergency stop and the emergency lowering procedure.
  • Training is given on induction, with a refresher every 3 years, and is recorded in the training record.
  • Hired vehicles: before first use, check the controls and emergency stop on that specific tail lift.
  • Operators sign the operator training and briefing record in SSOW-09 and the staff acknowledgement record in this SOP.

6. Equipment, PPE and materials

Item Requirement
Safety footwear Toe-capped safety footwear worn at all times (SSOW-03)
Hi-vis Worn, especially at the roadside and in loading areas
Gloves Good grip, for handling loads and straps
Tail lift Pre-use check passed; SWL and load centre plate legible; LOLER examination in date
Cones or barriers Carried in every tail lift vehicle to set up the exclusion zone
Platform warning lights or flags Working and used whenever the platform is deployed
Handling aids Pallet truck, sack truck or dolly suited to the load
Straps Available for tall or unstable loads
Vehicle check sheet To record the pre-use check

7. Procedure

Follow these steps in order each time the tail lift is used. If anything does not meet the standard, stop and report it.

7.1 Pre-use check (before first use each day)

  1. Check SWL and markings. Confirm the SWL and load centre plate is present and legible and the LOLER examination date is in date.
  2. Check the platform. Look for cracks, bends or damage; the surface must be anti-slip and free of oil, ice and debris.
  3. Check roll stops and guards. Roll stops must raise and lower correctly; handrails or safety barriers, where fitted, must be secure.
  4. Test the controls. All controls must work and return to off when released; two-handed or foot controls must work as designed; the emergency stop must work.
  5. Check the hydraulics. No leaks from hoses, rams or fittings; the platform must not creep down when held in position.
  6. Check the structure. Arms, hinges, pins and mounting bolts must be secure and undamaged.
  7. Check warning devices and power. Platform flashing lights or flags and the cab warning light must work; the battery and isolator switch must work.
  8. Record the check. Complete the vehicle check sheet.

Hold point: Any defect means the tail lift is not used. Isolate it, tag it “Do not use” and report it to the Warehouse Manager.

7.2 Site set-up

  1. Park correctly. Park on firm, level ground with the handbrake on, engine off (unless the tail lift needs the engine running) and the key removed.
  2. Check the space. Make sure there is enough room behind the vehicle for the platform to open and lower and for the load to be moved off it, with no overhead obstructions.
  3. Avoid poor ground. Do not use the tail lift on a slope, on soft or uneven ground, or near kerbs, drains and potholes.
  4. Set up the exclusion zone. Place cones or barriers behind the vehicle, especially at the roadside or in public areas, and use the platform warning lights or flags.
  5. Check the lighting. Make sure lighting is adequate for the work.

Hold point: Do not deploy the platform until the vehicle is on firm, level ground and the exclusion zone is in place.

7.3 Deploying the platform

  1. Switch on. Switch on the tail lift at the isolator or cab switch and check the cab warning light comes on.
  2. Clear the area. Make sure nobody is behind the vehicle or within the platform’s area of movement.
  3. Release the catches. Release any locking catches or safety chains, standing to the side, never directly behind the platform.
  4. Open and lower. Unfold the platform and lower it to the ground using the controls, watching it all the way down.
  5. Check and raise roll stops. Check the platform is lying flat and stable on the ground and raise the roll stops where fitted.

7.4 Loading the platform

  1. Check the weight. Confirm the load is within the SWL and its weight will sit at or inside the marked load centre. Include the weight of the pallet truck or trolley, and the operator if riding.
  2. Move the load on. Move the load onto the platform squarely and slowly using a pallet truck, sack truck or dolly as needed, and centre it away from the edges.
  3. Secure wheeled loads. Lower pallet truck forks fully so the load sits on the platform, apply the brake on cages or trolleys, and make sure the roll stops are up at the outer edge.
  4. Stabilise tall loads. Strap tall or unstable loads (stacked cases, panels, furniture) together, or have two people steady them from a safe position, never from below or in front.
  5. One load at a time. Carry only one load unless the platform is designed for more and the total is within SWL.

Hold point: Do not raise or lower the platform until the load is within SWL and the load centre, wheeled loads are braked or forks lowered, and the roll stops are up.

7.5 Raising and lowering

  1. Take the control position. Operate only from the designated control position, with a clear view of the platform and load.
  2. Keep feet and hands clear. Keep feet clear of the platform edge and away from underneath it; keep hands on the controls or handrail, away from hinges and arms.
  3. Operate smoothly. Use the hold-to-run controls smoothly and stop at once if anything moves, shifts or looks wrong.
  4. Ride only where permitted. Ride the platform only where the tail lift is designed and marked for an operator to ride: stand within the marked area, facing the vehicle, holding the handrail, feet well inside the edge. Never ride with a heavy wheeled load you could not hold if it moved; operate from the ground instead.
  5. Check level at bed height. When the platform reaches bed level, check it is level with the vehicle bed. Lower the roll stops only when you are ready to move the load.
  6. Load the vehicle. Move the load into the vehicle and secure it straight away (SOP-07 / SSOW-07, SOP-08 / SSOW-08).
  7. Unload in reverse. Move the load onto the platform, raise the roll stops, apply brakes, lower to the ground, and move the load away before raising the platform again.

Hold point: Do not move a load across between platform and vehicle until the platform is level with the vehicle bed.

7.6 Stowing and leaving

  1. Clear the platform. Remove all loads, straps and debris.
  2. Stow the platform. Lower the roll stops if they fold away, raise the platform and fold or slide it into the stowed position.
  3. Lock it. Fit the locking catches or safety chains and check the platform is fully stowed and secure.
  4. Switch off. Switch off at the isolator or cab switch and check the cab warning light is off.
  5. Clear the site. Remove the cones or barriers.

Hold point: Do not drive away until the platform is stowed and locked and the cab warning light is off.

8. Completion checks

Check Standard
Pre-use check Completed before first use that day and recorded on the vehicle check sheet
Load Moved into the vehicle and secured straight away, or moved clear of the platform when unloading
Platform Clear of loads, straps and debris
Stowage Platform fully stowed with locking catches or safety chains fitted
Power Tail lift switched off; cab warning light off
Site Cones or barriers removed; platform never left deployed and unattended in a public area
Defects Any defect tagged “Do not use” and reported to the Warehouse Manager the same day

9. If something goes wrong

Situation Action
Load starts to roll or topple Let go and step clear to the side; do not try to stop it with your body; shout a warning
Person trapped Press the emergency stop; call for help; if safe, use the controls or emergency lowering to free them; call 999 for any serious injury
Tail lift fails with a load raised Stop; keep everyone clear from under the platform; do not climb on it; use emergency lowering only if trained, otherwise call the maintenance provider
Platform will not stow Do not drive; make the area safe; call the maintenance provider
Defect found before or during use Stop using the tail lift; isolate it, tag it “Do not use” and report it to the Warehouse Manager
Accident or near miss Report to the Warehouse Manager the same day; the Managing Director reports RIDDOR-reportable incidents, including lifting equipment failure, to HSE

See SSOW-09 – Tail Lift Operation for the full emergency arrangements.

10. Records

Record Completed by Kept by
Vehicle check sheet (pre-use check, before first use each day) Operator Warehouse Manager
Service record (as manufacturer’s schedule and at vehicle safety inspections) Competent engineer Warehouse Manager
Report of thorough examination (LOLER, at least every 6 months; kept at least 2 years or until the next report) Competent person Warehouse Manager
Training record (induction; refresher every 3 years) Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
Accident, near miss and defect reports Operator Warehouse Manager
Staff acknowledgement record (this SOP) Each operator Warehouse Manager

documents.html:
Document details

This safe system of work sets out how Pickard Event Services plans, installs, tests, operates and removes temporary electrical installations at events: connection to venue or show supplies, power distribution units, cable runs and the equipment plugged into them. Temporary systems are put up and taken down quickly, often outdoors, in wet weather and among the public, so the main dangers are electric shock, fire from overloaded or damaged equipment, and trips over cable runs.

Generators are not covered by this SSOW. Where power comes from a generator, siting, earthing, fuelling and running the generator are covered by the separate Generator SSOW and SOP; this SSOW starts at the generator’s output connection.

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
Reference SSOW-10 – Temporary Electrical Installations
Equipment Venue and show supplies, power distribution units (PDUs) and distribution boards, RCD units, armoured and flexible cables (Powerlock, 125 A, 63 A, 32 A and 16 A BS EN 60309 ‘Ceeform’ connectors, 13 A), cable ramps and covers, lighting, AV and stand equipment, test instruments
Locations Event sites (indoor venues, exhibition halls, marquees and outdoor sites) and Unit 1, Brickyard Road (equipment preparation and storage)
Tasks Planning the power system; connecting to supplies; laying out distribution and cables; inspecting, testing and energising; monitoring during the event; isolating and removing the system at breakdown
Persons at risk Electricians, crew, other contractors, venue staff, performers, exhibitors, visitors and members of the public
Assessor James Pickard
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner after an accident or near miss, a change in the type of system or equipment used, or a change in regulations or standards

Key legislation and guidance: Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 (EAWR); Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999; Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER); Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 (CDM, which applies to event build and breakdown); Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005; BS 7671 Requirements for Electrical Installations (IET Wiring Regulations, current edition), in particular Section 711 (Exhibitions, shows and stands) and Section 740 (Temporary installations for structures, amusement devices and booths at fairgrounds and circuses); BS 7909 Code of practice for temporary electrical systems for entertainment and related purposes; HSE GS38 Electrical test equipment for use on low voltage electrical systems; HSE HSR25 Memorandum of guidance on the EAWR; The Event Safety Guide (the Purple Guide), electrical chapter.

Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Approves this SSOW; appoints a competent Responsible Person for each temporary system; makes sure electricians are qualified and test equipment is calibrated; provides resources
Responsible Person (qualified electrician in charge of the temporary system, as described in BS 7909) Designs or checks the power plan; supervises installation; carries out or oversees the full inspection and test of every installation; signs the certificate before the system is energised; controls who may switch, alter or isolate the system; is contactable throughout the event
Electricians (qualified and competent, in-house or subcontracted) Install, connect, test and remove the system to this SSOW; carry out safe isolation; record test results; report defects
Warehouse Manager Keeps cables, distribution and RCD units visually inspected, maintained and labelled; quarantines and repairs defective kit; keeps equipment records
Crew (non-electricians) Lay and remove cables and plug in equipment only as directed by the Responsible Person; never open distribution, connect to supplies or alter the system; carry out user checks on equipment; report damage straight away
Venue / event organiser Provides venue supply details and the event electrical requirements; agrees the power plan, access and emergency arrangements

Hazards and risk ratings

Risk = Likelihood (L) × Severity (S), each scored 1–5, as in the H-series risk assessments. Ratings are residual risk, with this SSOW followed. Electric shock, loss of earth, water ingress and unauthorised access to distribution carry the highest residual risk (5, Medium) because any failure could be fatal; trips over cable runs are the most likely injury.

Score Likelihood Severity
1 Very unlikely Trivial – no treatment needed
2 Unlikely Minor – first aid only
3 Possible Moderate – medical treatment, up to 7 days off work
4 Likely Major – RIDDOR-reportable or over-7-day injury
5 Almost certain Fatal or permanent disability
Risk score Rating Action required
1–4 Low Maintain current controls; review annually
5–9 Medium Controls adequate but monitor; improve where reasonably practicable
10–16 High Further controls needed before or alongside work; management attention
20–25 Very high Stop work until risk is reduced
Ref Hazard Main controls (stage of this SSOW) Residual L × S Rating
EL1 Electric shock from damaged cables, connectors or equipment Visual inspection before dispatch and user checks before use; full inspection and test of every installation before energising; 30 mA RCD protection on final circuits and socket outlets; damaged kit quarantined (Before work starts, Stages 4, 5, 6) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
EL2 Electric shock or arc burns when connecting to, or disconnecting from, a supply Connect and disconnect dead only; safe isolation, lock-off and prove dead with GS38 test equipment; no live working; correct connection sequence for Powerlock (Stages 2, 7) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
EL3 Loss of earth or incorrect earthing Earthing arrangement of each supply confirmed in the power plan; earth continuity, earth fault loop and RCD tests before energising (Stages 2, 5) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
EL4 Overloaded cables or distribution causing overheating and fire Load calculation in the power plan; correctly rated protective devices; cable drums fully unwound; load checks during the event (Stages 4, 6) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
EL5 Water, rain and flooding reaching live parts IP44 or better outdoors; connectors and distribution raised off the ground and covered; drip loops; plan for weather; stop in lightning (Stages 3, 4, 6) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
EL6 Trips and falls over cable runs Routes planned away from walkways and exits; cable ramps, covers or matting; cables taped, marked or flown overhead (Stage 4) 2 × 2 = 4 Low
EL7 Cables crushed or cut by vehicles, forklifts, staging or ballast Cable ramps rated for vehicles at crossings; cables run after heavy build where possible; re-inspection after build (Stages 4, 5) 1 × 4 = 4 Low
EL8 Unauthorised access to, or alteration of, distribution by crew, exhibitors or the public Distribution locked, guarded or out of reach; warning signs; only the Responsible Person authorises connections and changes (Stages 3, 6) 1 × 5 = 5 Medium
EL9 Manual handling of heavy cables and distribution units Team lifts; trolleys or pallet trucks for heavy items; cables coiled to manageable weights (H8; Stages 1, 4, 7) 2 × 2 = 4 Low
EL10 Working at height to run cables over trusses, structures or ceilings Planned access with suitable equipment (H5); cables secured to support wires, not hung from structures not designed for them (Stage 4) 1 × 4 = 4 Low

Before work starts

Competence and authorisation

  • Electrical work (connecting to supplies and distribution, making or altering circuits, testing, isolation) is done only by qualified, competent electricians: a recognised electrical qualification, current BS 7671 knowledge and experience of temporary event systems (BS 7909 training recommended). Subcontracted electricians provide evidence of competence and insurance before the event.
  • A Responsible Person is named for every temporary system, on the power plan, and is contactable for the whole event, from first connection to final removal.
  • Crew may lay and remove cables, place cable ramps and plug equipment into outlets provided for them, but only when briefed and directed by the Responsible Person. Crew never open distribution units or connect to supplies.

Planning (Responsible Person, before the event)

  1. Obtain the supply details (type, rating, location and earthing arrangement) and the event power requirements from the venue, organiser, exhibitors and suppliers. Where a generator is used, agree its output connection and earthing with whoever is responsible for it under the Generator SSOW.
  2. Prepare a power plan: supply, earthing arrangement, distribution layout, cable routes and sizes, protective devices and RCDs, and a load calculation with spare capacity.
  3. Plan cable routes away from walkways, fire exits, vehicle routes and public areas where possible; identify crossing points needing ramps or flown cables.
  4. Agree the power plan, isolation points and emergency arrangements with the venue or organiser, and share them with the event safety team.
  5. Check the weather forecast for outdoor events and plan for rain, standing water, wind and lightning.
  6. Prepare the equipment list, and allow time in the schedule for the full inspection and test before anything is energised.

Equipment preparation (warehouse, before dispatch)

Every installation is fully inspected and tested on site before it is energised (Stage 5), so equipment is not PAT tested separately. Before dispatch, equipment is visually checked. Any defect = equipment not sent. Quarantine it, tag it “Do not use” and report it to the Warehouse Manager.

Item Check
Cables and leads Sheath undamaged, no cuts, crushing, taped joins or exposed inner cores; cable grips secure
Connectors Correct type and rating; pins and sleeves undamaged and clean; caps and seals present; IP rating suitable for outdoor use where needed
Distribution units and RCD units Casing, glands and doors undamaged; labels correct; no signs of overheating or water ingress
Test equipment Multifunction tester and voltage indicator in calibration; GS38-compliant leads, probes and fused leads; proving unit working
Ancillaries Cable ramps, covers and matting; lock-off kits and padlocks; warning signs and “Do not switch on” tags; CO2 fire extinguisher

Personal protective equipment

  • Safety footwear and hi-vis (SSOW-03), with hard hats where there is overhead work.
  • Gloves for handling cables; insulated gloves only where the Responsible Person’s method requires them.

Safe system of work – step by step

Stage 1 – Arrival and set-out

  1. Sign in, attend the venue or site induction, and confirm the emergency arrangements, first aid and the location of the venue’s main isolation points.
  2. Walk the site with the power plan. Check supply positions, distribution positions and cable routes are still suitable, and agree any changes with the Responsible Person before work starts.
  3. Check ground conditions: firm, level and free of standing water where distribution will go.
  4. Unload equipment (H8, SSOW-06, SSOW-09) and check it for transit damage. Anything damaged is set aside and tagged “Do not use”.

Stage 2 – Connecting to supplies

  1. Venue supplies: agree the connection with the venue electrician. The venue supply is isolated, locked off and proved dead (GS38 voltage indicator, proved on a known source before and after) before anything is connected. The venue switches on only when the Responsible Person asks.
  2. Generator supplies: connect only once the generator is set up, earthed and stopped or isolated under the Generator SSOW, and the person responsible for it has agreed.
  3. Connect dead only. For single-pole connectors (Powerlock), connect in the order earth, neutral, then phases, and check each is fully locked. Never connect or disconnect high-current connectors under load or live.

Stage 3 – Distribution

  1. Position distribution units on firm ground, raised off the floor where water could collect, out of walkways and away from public reach, or inside a locked enclosure. Outdoors, use units with a suitable IP rating and covers.
  2. Lock or guard distribution and fit “Danger – electricity” signs. Label each unit with its supply and its outgoing circuits.
  3. Keep all outgoing breakers off, and lock off any circuit that people are still working on.

Stage 4 – Cable runs and final circuits

  1. Lay cables along the planned routes, keeping clear of fire exits, escape routes and doors. Never run cables through doors that can close on them.
  2. Unwind cable drums fully. Lay surplus cable flat in a figure of eight; never leave it tightly coiled, bundled or covered by insulating materials, where it can overheat.
  3. At walkway and vehicle crossings, use cable ramps rated for the traffic, or fly cables overhead on a support wire at a height agreed with the venue, clear of vehicles and plant.
  4. Keep connectors off the ground and out of water; form drip loops so water runs away from connectors and equipment. Outdoors, use only IP-rated connectors and enclosures.
  5. Secure and mark cables: tape edges or use matting in public areas, and fix flown cables to support wires, never to structures not designed to carry them (work at height to H5).
  6. Protect all final circuits and socket outlets with 30 mA RCDs, and give each stand or area an accessible means of isolation, as set out in the power plan.

Stage 5 – Inspection, testing and energising

  1. The Responsible Person walks the whole system: supplies, earthing, distribution, cable routes, connectors and protection, checking it matches the power plan and that every cable, connector and unit is undamaged.
  2. Carry out dead tests before energising: protective conductor continuity, insulation resistance and polarity.
  3. Warn everyone that the system is about to go live and clear people from distribution and connection points. Energise in stages, from the source outwards.
  4. Carry out live tests: earth fault loop impedance, RCD operation and trip times, phase rotation and voltages. Correct any fault before the circuit is used.
  5. Record the results and complete and sign the electrical certificate for the temporary system (BS 7671 / BS 7909) before the system is handed over. Nothing is used by exhibitors, performers or the public until it is signed.
  6. Brief crew, exhibitors and suppliers on what they may plug in, where, the loads allowed, where the isolation points are, and who to call with a problem.

Stage 6 – During the event

  1. The Responsible Person (or a named competent electrician) stays on site or on call, and checks the system at regular intervals: cable damage, heat at connectors and distribution, water, and loads against the plan.
  2. Only the Responsible Person may authorise new connections, extra loads or changes. Anything altered is inspected and tested again before use, and the records are updated.
  3. If an RCD or breaker trips, find and remove the cause before resetting. Never reset repeatedly, bypass an RCD or fit a higher-rated device.
  4. Weather: if water reaches live parts, isolate that part of the system. In lightning, follow the event’s weather plan and keep people away from distribution and flown cables outdoors.

Stage 7 – Breakdown and removal

  1. Agree with the organiser when power can be switched off, and warn everyone affected before isolating.
  2. Switch off and isolate from the final circuits back towards the source. Lock off the supply (or have it isolated under the Generator SSOW), and prove dead at the distribution before disconnecting anything.
  3. Disconnect in reverse order. For Powerlock, phases first, then neutral, then earth last.
  4. Remove cables only once they are disconnected and dead. Coil them to manageable weights, inspect them as they are rolled up, and tag damaged items “Do not use”.
  5. Return all equipment to Unit 1, Brickyard Road, and report defects to the Warehouse Manager so items are repaired before reuse.

Never

  • Never carry out electrical work unless you are a qualified, competent electrician authorised by the Responsible Person.
  • Never work on, connect to or disconnect from live equipment; isolate, lock off and prove dead first.
  • Never energise any part of the system before it has been fully inspected, tested and certified.
  • Never use damaged equipment, or repair cables with tape.
  • Never bypass, override or reset an RCD or breaker without finding the cause of the trip.
  • Never leave connectors or distribution lying in water, or use indoor-rated equipment outdoors.
  • Never run cables across fire exits or escape routes, or leave unprotected cables across walkways or vehicle routes.
  • Never leave distribution unlocked or unguarded where the public, exhibitors or untrained crew can reach it.
  • Never use water on an electrical fire.

Emergencies

Situation Action
Electric shock Do not touch the casualty until the supply is isolated; switch off at the nearest isolator; if you cannot isolate, move them clear with dry non-conductive material only; call 999; start CPR and use the defibrillator if they are not breathing normally
Electrical fire Raise the alarm; isolate the supply if it is safe to do so; use a CO2 extinguisher only if trained and safe; never water; evacuate and call 999 (H19)
Damaged cable or exposed live parts Keep people back; isolate that circuit; cordon off the area; call the Responsible Person; replace the item; inspect and test before re-energising
Water reaching live parts or flooding Isolate the affected part of the system; keep people away; do not re-energise until it is dried, inspected and tested
Loss of power during the event Tell the event control and the Responsible Person; keep people calm and use emergency lighting; find the cause before restoring power in stages

All accidents, near misses and defects are reported to the Responsible Person and the Warehouse Manager the same day and recorded. RIDDOR-reportable incidents, including electrical short circuits or overloads that cause a fire or explosion, are reported to HSE by the Managing Director.

Inspection and records

Item Frequency By whom Record
Power plan and load calculation Before each event Responsible Person Power plan, kept with the event file
Visual inspection of cables, leads, distribution and RCD units Before dispatch and on return Warehouse Manager Defects tagged “Do not use” and logged for repair
Equipment user checks Before each use Electricians and crew Report defects; tag “Do not use”
Full inspection and testing of the temporary system After every installation, before energising, and after any alteration Responsible Person Electrical certificate and schedule of test results, kept with the event file
Checks during the event At regular intervals while the system is live Responsible Person Event log
Test instrument calibration At least annually Managing Director (arranges) Calibration certificate
Electrician competence Before each event for subcontractors; annually for in-house staff Managing Director Qualifications, insurance and training records

Related documents

  • Generator SSOW and SOP (separate documents)
  • H5 – Working at Height
  • H8 – Manual Handling
  • H19 – Fire Risk Assessment
  • SSOW-03 – Personal Protective Equipment
  • SSOW-06 – Pallet Truck
  • SSOW-09 – Tail Lift Operation
  • Event power plan and electrical certificate (for each event)

Action plan

Document control

Item Detail
Company JNM Events Ltd t/a Pickard Event Services
SOP reference SOP-10 – Temporary Electrical Installations
Linked SSOW SSOW-10 – Temporary Electrical Installations
Version 1.0
Prepared by James Pickard (Managing Director)
Approved by Mathew Pickard (Director)
Date issued Jan 2026
Next review Jan 2027, or sooner if SSOW-10 changes, after an accident or near miss, or when the equipment or task changes

1. Purpose

This SOP gives the standard method for planning, installing, testing, operating and removing temporary electrical installations at events. It makes clear which steps are electrical work, done only by qualified electricians under the Responsible Person, and which steps crew may carry out when directed. The hazards, risk ratings and controls are in SSOW-10 – Temporary Electrical Installations, which must be read with this SOP.

2. Scope

This SOP covers every temporary electrical system we install at events, from planning and equipment preparation to connection, installation, full inspection and testing, energising, monitoring, and isolation and removal at breakdown. Generators are covered by the separate Generator SSOW and SOP; where power comes from a generator, this procedure starts at the generator’s output connection.

Applies to:

  • The Responsible Person, electricians (in-house and subcontracted), crew and the Warehouse Manager.
  • Event sites (indoor venues, exhibition halls, marquees and outdoor sites) and Unit 1, Brickyard Road (equipment preparation and storage).
  • Venue and show supplies, PDUs and distribution boards, RCD units, cables and connectors (Powerlock, 125 A, 63 A, 32 A and 16 A BS EN 60309 ‘Ceeform’, 13 A), cable ramps and covers, lighting, AV and stand equipment, and test instruments.

Does not cover:

  • Generators, up to their output connection (Generator SSOW and SOP, separate documents).
  • PPE selection and use in general (SOP-03 / SSOW-03).
  • Moving and unloading equipment with pallet trucks or tail lifts (SOP-06 / SSOW-06, SOP-09 / SSOW-09).
  • Access equipment for work at height (H5).
  • Switching of the venue’s own supply, which the venue electrician does when the Responsible Person asks.

3. Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Managing Director (James Pickard) Appoints a competent Responsible Person for each system; checks electricians are qualified and test equipment calibrated; provides resources; reports RIDDOR incidents to HSE
Responsible Person (qualified electrician in charge, BS 7909) Prepares or checks the power plan; supervises installation; carries out or oversees the full inspection and test of every installation; signs the certificate before energising; controls who may switch, alter or isolate; directs crew; stays contactable throughout the event
Electricians Install, connect, test and remove the system; carry out safe isolation; record test results; report defects
Warehouse Manager Visually inspects cables, distribution and RCD units before dispatch and on return; keeps them maintained and labelled; quarantines and repairs defective kit; keeps equipment records
Crew (non-electricians) Lay and remove cables, place ramps and plug in equipment only as directed by the Responsible Person; carry out user checks; report damage straight away; never open distribution, connect to supplies or alter the system
Venue / event organiser Provides supply details and power requirements; agrees the power plan, access and emergency arrangements

4. Definitions

Term Meaning
Responsible Person The qualified electrician named on the power plan as in charge of the temporary system
Electrical work Connecting to supplies and distribution, making or altering circuits, testing and isolation. Electricians only
Power plan Supply, earthing arrangement, distribution layout, cable routes and sizes, protective devices, RCDs and load calculation for the event
Safe isolation Isolate, lock off and prove dead with a GS38 voltage indicator, proved on a known source before and after
Full inspection and test The Responsible Person’s on-site inspection, dead tests and live tests of every installation before it is energised, recorded on the electrical certificate
Powerlock Single-pole high-current connectors, connected and disconnected dead in a set order
Electrical certificate The signed certificate and schedule of test results for the temporary system (BS 7671 / BS 7909)

5. Competence and authorisation

  • Only qualified, competent electricians carry out electrical work: a recognised electrical qualification, current BS 7671 knowledge and experience of temporary event systems (BS 7909 training recommended).
  • Subcontracted electricians provide evidence of competence and insurance before each event; in-house competence is checked annually by the Managing Director.
  • A Responsible Person is named on the power plan for every system and is contactable from first connection to final removal.
  • Crew may lay and remove cables, place cable ramps and plug equipment into outlets provided for them, only when briefed and directed by the Responsible Person.
  • All electricians and crew are briefed on SSOW-10 and sign the briefing record.

6. Equipment, PPE and materials

Item Requirement
Cables, leads and connectors Visually checked and undamaged; correct type and rating; caps and seals present; IP44 or better outdoors
Distribution and RCD units Casing, glands, doors and labels undamaged; no signs of overheating or water ingress; lockable enclosure or guard; warning signs
Test equipment Multifunction tester and voltage indicator in calibration; GS38-compliant leads, probes and fused leads; proving unit
Isolation kit Lock-off kits, padlocks, “Do not switch on” and “Do not use” tags
Cable protection Ramps rated for the traffic, covers, matting, tape, support wires
Fire extinguisher CO2 extinguisher for electrical fires
PPE Safety footwear and hi-vis (SOP-03); hard hat for overhead work; gloves for handling cables; insulated gloves only where the Responsible Person’s method requires them

7. Procedure

Follow the phases in order. Each heading states who carries out that phase. If you are not named, do not do it.

7.1 Planning (Responsible Person, before the event)

  1. Get the supply details. Obtain the supply type, rating, location and earthing arrangement, and the power needs of the venue, organiser, exhibitors and suppliers.
  2. Agree any generator output connection. Where a generator is used, agree its output connection and earthing with whoever is responsible for it under the Generator SSOW.
  3. Prepare the power plan. Include all items in the definition above, with spare capacity in the load calculation. Route cables away from walkways, fire exits, vehicle routes and public areas, and mark crossings needing ramps or flown cables.
  4. Agree and share the plan. Agree the plan, isolation points and emergency arrangements with the venue or organiser and share them with the event safety team.
  5. Plan for weather and testing. Check the forecast for rain, standing water, wind and lightning. Prepare the equipment list and allow time for the full inspection and test before anything is energised.

7.2 Equipment preparation (Warehouse Manager, before dispatch)

  1. Visually check cables and connectors. No cuts, crushing, taped joins or exposed cores; cable grips secure; correct type and rating; pins and sleeves clean and undamaged; caps and seals present; IP rating suitable for outdoors where needed.
  2. Visually check distribution and RCD units. Casing, glands and doors undamaged; labels correct; no signs of overheating or water ingress.
  3. Check test equipment and ancillaries. Testers in calibration with GS38-compliant leads and a working proving unit; ramps, covers, matting, lock-off kits, signs, tags and CO2 extinguisher packed.
  4. Quarantine defects. Do not send any item with a defect. Tag it “Do not use” and report it to the Warehouse Manager for repair.

Hold point: No item leaves Unit 1, Brickyard Road with a visible defect.

7.3 Arrival and set-out (all staff; changes agreed by the Responsible Person)

  1. Sign in and induct. Attend the induction and confirm emergency arrangements, first aid and the venue’s main isolation points.
  2. Walk the site with the power plan. Confirm supply and distribution positions and cable routes are still suitable; agree any change with the Responsible Person first.
  3. Check the ground. Distribution positions must be firm, level and free of standing water.
  4. Unload and check. Unload to H8, SOP-06 and SOP-09, using team lifts, trolleys or pallet trucks for heavy items. Set aside anything damaged in transit and tag it “Do not use”.

7.4 Connecting to supplies (electricians only)

  1. Isolate the venue supply. Agree the connection with the venue electrician. The supply is isolated, locked off and proved dead with a GS38 voltage indicator, proved on a known source before and after.
  2. Confirm any generator supply is ready. Connect only once the generator is set up, earthed and stopped or isolated under the Generator SSOW, and the person responsible for it has agreed.
  3. Connect dead only. For Powerlock, connect earth, then neutral, then phases, checking each is fully locked. Never connect or disconnect high-current connectors live or under load.
  4. Switch on only on request. The venue switches on only when the Responsible Person asks.

Hold point: Nothing is connected to any supply until it has been isolated, locked off and proved dead.

7.5 Distribution (electricians only)

  1. Position distribution. On firm ground, raised where water could collect, out of walkways and public reach or in a locked enclosure; IP-rated with covers outdoors.
  2. Secure and label. Lock or guard each unit, fit “Danger – electricity” signs and label each unit with its supply and outgoing circuits.
  3. Keep outgoing breakers off. Lock off any circuit people are still working on.

7.6 Cable runs and final circuits (crew lay cables as directed; electricians connect and protect)

  1. Lay cables on the planned routes. Keep clear of fire exits, escape routes and doors; never run cables through doors that can close on them.
  2. Unwind drums fully. Lay surplus flat in a figure of eight; never leave it tightly coiled, bundled or covered, where it can overheat.
  3. Protect crossings. Use ramps rated for the traffic, or fly cables on a support wire at a height agreed with the venue, clear of vehicles and plant. Run cables after heavy build where possible.
  4. Keep connectors dry. Keep connectors off the ground and out of water, form drip loops, and use only IP-rated connectors and enclosures outdoors.
  5. Secure and mark cables. Tape edges or use matting in public areas; fix flown cables to support wires, never to structures not designed for them (H5). Use team lifts for heavy cables (H8).
  6. Fit RCDs and isolation (electricians). Protect all final circuits and socket outlets with 30 mA RCDs and give each stand or area an accessible means of isolation, per the power plan.

7.7 Full inspection, testing and energising (Responsible Person and electricians)

  1. Walk the whole system. The Responsible Person checks supplies, earthing, distribution, cable routes, connectors and protection match the power plan and that every cable, connector and unit is undamaged, including after heavy build.
  2. Carry out dead tests. Protective conductor continuity, insulation resistance and polarity.
  3. Warn, clear and energise in stages. Tell everyone the system is going live, clear people from distribution and connection points, and energise from the source outwards.
  4. Carry out live tests. Earth fault loop impedance, RCD operation and trip times, phase rotation and voltages. Correct any fault before the circuit is used.
  5. Record and certify. Record the results and complete and sign the electrical certificate before handover.
  6. Brief users. Tell crew, exhibitors and suppliers what they may plug in and where, permitted loads, isolation points and who to call with a problem.

Hold point: Nothing is used by crew, exhibitors, performers or the public until the full inspection and test is complete and the Responsible Person has signed the certificate.

7.8 During the event (Responsible Person; crew user checks)

  1. Check at regular intervals. The Responsible Person, or a named competent electrician, stays on site or on call and checks for cable damage, heat at connectors and distribution, water, and loads against the plan. Record checks in the event log.
  2. Control changes. Only the Responsible Person authorises new connections, extra loads or changes; anything altered is inspected and tested again and the records updated before use.
  3. Check before plugging in (crew). Carry out user checks on equipment before use and report any damage straight away.
  4. Deal with trips. If an RCD or breaker trips, an electrician finds and removes the cause before resetting. Never reset repeatedly, bypass an RCD or fit a higher-rated device.
  5. Act on weather. If water reaches live parts, isolate that part of the system. In lightning, follow the event weather plan and keep people away from distribution and outdoor flown cables.

Hold point: A tripped RCD or breaker is not reset until the cause has been found and removed.

7.9 Breakdown and removal (electricians isolate; crew remove cables when directed)

  1. Agree switch-off. Agree timing with the organiser and warn everyone affected before isolating.
  2. Isolate and prove dead (electricians). Switch off from the final circuits back towards the source. Lock off the supply, or have a generator supply isolated under the Generator SSOW, and prove dead at the distribution.
  3. Disconnect in reverse order (electricians). For Powerlock, phases first, then neutral, then earth last.
  4. Remove cables (crew, when directed). Start only when the Responsible Person confirms cables are disconnected and dead. Coil to manageable weights, inspect while rolling up and tag damaged items “Do not use”.
  5. Return and report. Return all equipment to Unit 1, Brickyard Road. The Warehouse Manager visually inspects it on return, and defective items are repaired before reuse.

Hold point: Nothing is disconnected or removed until it has been isolated, locked off and proved dead.

8. Completion checks

Check Standard
Power plan Agreed with the venue or organiser and kept with the event file
Supply connection Made dead, in the correct Powerlock sequence, with each connector locked
Distribution Locked or guarded, signed, labelled, off wet ground and out of public reach
Cable runs Clear of exits and escape routes; crossings ramped or flown; connectors dry and raised
Protection 30 mA RCDs on all final circuits and socket outlets; isolation for each stand or area
Certification Full inspection and test recorded and certificate signed before use; retested after any alteration
Breakdown Isolated before disconnection; equipment visually inspected on return and defects reported

9. If something goes wrong

Situation Action
Electric shock Do not touch the casualty until the supply is isolated; switch off at the nearest isolator; if you cannot, move them clear with dry non-conductive material only; call 999; start CPR and use the defibrillator if not breathing normally
Electrical fire Raise the alarm; isolate the supply if safe; use a CO2 extinguisher only if trained and safe; never water; evacuate and call 999 (H19)
Damaged cable or exposed live parts Keep people back; isolate the circuit; cordon off the area; call the Responsible Person; replace the item; inspect and test before re-energising
Water on live parts or flooding Isolate the affected part; keep people away; do not re-energise until dried, inspected and tested
Loss of power during the event Tell event control and the Responsible Person; keep people calm and use emergency lighting; find the cause before restoring power in stages
Accident, near miss or defect Report to the Responsible Person and Warehouse Manager the same day and record it; the Managing Director reports RIDDOR incidents to HSE

The full emergency arrangements are in SSOW-10 – Temporary Electrical Installations.

10. Records

Record Completed by Kept by

Visual inspection defects, tagged “Do not use” and logged for repair (before dispatch and on return) Warehouse Manager Warehouse Manager
User check defect reports (before each use) Electricians and crew Warehouse Manager

Event log of checks while live Responsible Person Event file
Test instrument calibration certificate (at least annually) Arranged by Managing Director Managing Director
Electrician qualifications, insurance and training (subcontractors before each event; in-house annually) Managing Director Managing Director
Accident, near miss and defect reports Person involved Responsible Person and Warehouse Manager
